What’s On Tonight

Samba do Trabalhador at the Renascença Clube — Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí. Every Monday for more than twenty years, composer Moacyr Luz and his group have run this roda — born as a party for musicians on their one night off, now a Rio institution. The house opens at 4:30 pm and the samba runs in three sets to about 10 pm, to a packed, dancing terrace. Tickets are R$30 (US$6) in advance through Sympla or R$40 (US$8) on the door, and there is a R$30 (US$6) solidarity ticket if you bring a kilo of non-perishable food. All ages are welcome and under-11s go free. Bring cash for the bar. Come early — it fills.

The Pedra do Sal roda, back tonight — Largo João da Baiana, Saúde. Monday is the flagship night for the free open-air roda at the birthplace of Carioca samba. Musicians play at the foot of the old stone steps and the crowd fills the largo, from 7 pm to around midnight. Free to attend, with drinks bought using cash tokens sold on the spot — the perfect after-dark follow-on to an afternoon in Andaraí, or a night out on its own.

Beco do Rato — Rua Joaquim Silva 11, Lapa. The Lapa house that actually opens on a Monday: a small, unfussy samba bar with live music every night of the week, doors from 6 pm to 1 am. Tickets are sold through Sympla, so check the night’s act before you go. A reliable indoor option if you want to end the night in Lapa.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Late afternoon (4:30–5 pm) — Doors at the Renascença Clube in Andaraí for Samba do Trabalhador. This is the main event; give it the afternoon.

Early evening (7 pm) — As the Andaraí roda winds down, the free Pedra do Sal roda gets going in the port.

Night (from 8 pm) — Samba at Beco do Rato in Lapa, a short ride from the port.

Late (from 10 pm) — Bip Bip in Copacabana for the tail of the Monday choro roda. No cover.

Getting home — Book a car rather than hunting for a late bus. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — The whole of a Rio Monday. Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí is the marquee; Pedra do Sal and Beco do Rato carry the night. Where: Renascença (Andaraí), Largo João da Baiana (Saúde), Beco do Rato (Rua Joaquim Silva 11).

Street samba — Monday is Pedra do Sal’s flagship night: free, open-air, at the birthplace of the genre. Where: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde.

Copacabana — Monday is choro night at Bip Bip, a low-key end to the evening. Where: Bip Bip (Rua Almirante Gonçalves 50).

Culture — CCBB Rio is open on Mondays (closed Tuesdays) with the free Vik Muniz show “A Olho Nu”, running to 12 October, until 8 pm. Where: CCBB (Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro).

Closed tonight — Rio Scenarium runs Wednesday to Saturday and Carioca da Gema Tuesday to Saturday — neither opens on a Monday. Where: back from Tuesday and Wednesday.

Pick Your Night

The one to beat: Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí — Rio’s great Monday roda.

Free and iconic: The Pedra do Sal roda on its flagship Monday night.

Indoor and reliable: Beco do Rato — the Lapa samba bar that opens on a Monday.

Low-key late: Bip Bip in Copacabana.

Culture first: The Vik Muniz show at CCBB, open on a Monday.

Where to Go

Renascença Clube — Andaraí A cultural club in the north-side neighbourhood of Andaraí, home every Monday to Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador — one of Rio’s essential samba experiences. Tonight: Samba do Trabalhador with Moacyr Luz. Doors 4:30 pm; three sets to about 10 pm. Best time: Every Monday. Arrive close to doors for a table on the terrace. Cost: R$30 (US$6) in advance through Sympla, R$40 (US$8) on the door; a R$30 (US$6) solidarity ticket with a kilo of food. All ages; under-11s free. Address: Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí Tickets: sympla.com.br Getting there: Rideshare is easiest; it’s north of the centre. Metro to Saens Peña, then a short ride. Good to know: Loud and joyful — buy ahead online, bring notes for the bar and, if you’re sensitive to volume, ear plugs. Confirm on the group’s Instagram.

Pedra do Sal — Saúde (Pequena África) The stone steps in the old port where Carioca samba was born. A free, open-air roda with a loose, street-party energy — at its biggest on a Monday. Tonight: The flagship Monday roda, from about 7 pm. Musicians at the foot of the steps; crowd across the largo. Best time: Mondays and Fridays are the big nights. Come early for a spot on the steps. Cost: Free to attend. Drinks on a cash token system — carry small bills. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde Getting there: VLT to the port, or metro Uruguaiana and a short walk/ride. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Wear comfortable shoes and keep an eye on your belongings in the crowd.

Beco do Rato — Lapa A small, unfussy samba bar just off the Lapa arches — live music every night of the week, and the neighbourhood’s dependable Monday option. Tonight: Live samba from around 8 pm, doors 6 pm to 1 am. Check the night’s act before you go. Best time: Open every night; a calmer, more local feel early in the week. Cost: Ticketed through Sympla; the weeknight cover is modest. Card and cash. Address: Rua Joaquim Silva 11, Lapa Website: becodorato.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, then a short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door at night. Good to know: A handy indoor option to pair with the Pedra do Sal roda, a short ride away.

Bip Bip — Copacabana A hole-in-the-wall Copacabana legend where the music is sacred. A different genre each night — choro on Mondays and Tuesdays — with players in a circle and the crowd on the pavement. Tonight: Monday is choro night — the roda gets going around 8 pm. Best time: From about 8–9 pm. Get there early for a plastic chair. Cost: No cover; drinks on an honesty-style tab. Cash. Bring small notes. Address: Rua Almirante Gonçalves 50, Loja D, Copacabana Getting there: Metro Cantagalo, about a five-minute walk, or Siqueira Campos. Good to know: The house rule is silence while the musicians play — respect it.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Andaraí / Tijuca (north side): Residential and local, home to the Renascença Clube. Come for the samba; rideshare in and out after dark.

Centro / Saúde / Gamboa: The old port and the cradle of samba, alive tonight for the Pedra do Sal roda. Quiet otherwise — travel by car.

Lapa: Mostly quiet on a Monday, but Beco do Rato keeps the samba going a short walk from the Arcos.

Copacabana: Home to Bip Bip and an easy beachfront base. Walkable and lively.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. Charming and low-key; rideshare up and down.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

A quiet Monday — Rio’s big queer club nights run Friday to Sunday. Tonight is calmer, and the samba rodas are the easy, mixed, welcoming option.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Samba do Trabalhador, Pedra do Sal and Beco do Rato are all broadly mixed and welcoming any night.

Money & How Paying Works Carry cash: Pedra do Sal’s drink tokens are cash-only and the bars at the rodas prefer notes. About R$150 (US$30) in small bills covers the night. Entry: Samba do Trabalhador is R$30 (US$6) in advance or R$40 (US$8) on the door, with a R$30 (US$6) solidarity ticket for a kilo of food; Pedra do Sal is free; Beco do Rato is ticketed through Sympla. Cards and Pix: Tickets for Samba do Trabalhador and Beco do Rato are sold online in advance, but assume cash at the rodas and street stalls. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. Check before adding more.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: MetrôRio runs roughly 5 am to midnight Monday to Saturday. Check the last-train time for your line before you rely on it.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and the safest way to and from Andaraí and the port. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Andaraí and the port: Both are residential or quiet at night — book a car door-to-door rather than walking to find one.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Copacabana: Well-lit and busy near the beachfront, but keep the usual awareness on quieter side streets after dark.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Samba do Trabalhador on every Monday?

Yes — it has run every Monday at the Renascença Clube for more than twenty years. It’s an afternoon-into-evening event (doors 4:30 pm), so plan to arrive early. Confirm on the group’s Instagram before a long trip across town.

Samba do Trabalhador or Pedra do Sal?

You can do both. Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí is a late-afternoon, ticketed, seated-terrace event that winds down by 10 pm; the free Pedra do Sal roda in the port gets going at 7 pm and runs to around midnight. Andaraí first, then the port, makes a perfect Monday.

Is Pedra do Sal really on tonight?

Yes — Monday is its flagship roda night, and it also runs Friday through Sunday. It’s free and open-air at Largo João da Baiana in Saúde, from 7 pm to around midnight.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not at all. The music does the work and the crowds are welcoming. A smile, a cold beer, and cash for the entry or the drinks are all you need.

Sources: Samba do Trabalhador (official), Riotur (Samba do Trabalhador), Riotur (Pedra do Sal), becodorato.com.br, CCBB Rio

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 17, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Live Music at Centro da Terra Monday is São Paulo’s quietest night, and the dependable move is Centro da Terra in Perdizes — an intimate room that runs Monday residencies through August. Tonight it is Sara Não Tem Nome, joined by Lorena Hollander, Marina Mole and Vladimir Safatle, from 8 pm. Small, curated and music-first, it’s the antidote to a dead Monday. Book ahead; the room is tiny.

Tonight at a Glance —Centro da Terra · Perdizes Sara Não Tem Nome’s August residency, with three guests tonight. From 8 pm; tickets from R$56 (US$11). —Bar Templo · Mooca Doce Encontro brings pagode to the east side, doors 8 pm. R$35 (US$7) standing, booked ahead. Over-18s. —CCBB São Paulo · Centro Open on Mondays (closed Tuesdays). No exhibition on right now — but the free MIACENA festival runs here to 22 August. —The week resets SP2B, SPIM and two Cinemateca seasons wrapped yesterday. MIACENA runs to 22 August, and the Kinoforum short-film festival opens Thursday. —Dark tonight: Casa de Francisca, Blue Note, JazzB and the Barra Funda clubs are all closed on a Monday.

Tonight, Monday 17 August 2026, São Paulo exhales. After a fortnight of festivals — SP2B, SPIM and two Cinemateca seasons all closed yesterday — the city is back to its quietest night of the week. That’s no bad thing: Monday is for intimate rooms. Centro da Terra runs its August residency in Perdizes, Bar Templo has pagode in the Mooca, and CCBB keeps its doors open in the centre for the MIACENA festival. A calm, low-key night before the week builds again.

The city’s theatres and small rooms carry a São Paulo Monday. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Centro da Terra — Rua Piracuama 19, Perdizes. A small, much-loved room that programmes Monday residencies of indie, MPB and experimental music, running a single artist across several weeks. August belongs to Sara Não Tem Nome, whose Não Tem Nome season runs every Monday of the month at 8 pm; tonight she is joined by Lorena Hollander, Marina Mole and Vladimir Safatle. The venue prices on a sliding scale — R$112 (US$22) is the reference full price, and it releases 40% of seats at R$56 (US$11) or less. Book ahead through Sympla; capacity is small.

Bar Templo — Mooca. Over on the east side, Bar Templo puts on Doce Encontro tonight, doors at 8 pm — a relaxed, sociable pagode evening away from the tourist trail. The standing ticket is R$35 (US$7) through Clube do Ingresso; table and bistro places run R$170 (US$33) to R$260 (US$50) and several are already sold out. Over-18s only, and Monday shows here are frequent but not weekly, so check the date.

CCBB São Paulo — Rua Álvares Penteado 112, Centro. One of the few big cultural venues open on a Monday (it closes Tuesdays instead), in a beautiful restored building. There is no exhibition in the galleries at the moment — the last one closed on 3 August — but MIACENA, a free international performing-arts festival, runs here until 22 August. Tonight’s session is a free panel on how festivals build communities, at 5 pm in the theatre. A good early-evening stop before a quiet dinner.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Late afternoon (5 pm) — The free MIACENA panel at CCBB in the centre; the building closes at 8 pm.

Dinner (8 pm) — Eat in Perdizes or Pinheiros, close to Centro da Terra.

Main event (8 pm) — Sara Não Tem Nome at Centro da Terra, or pagode at Bar Templo in the Mooca.

Nightcap (10–11 pm) — A bar in Pinheiros or Vila Madalena; both keep a few doors open midweek.

Note — Monday is not a club night in São Paulo. Save Barra Funda for the weekend.

Scenes & Sounds

Intimate live music — Monday belongs to the small rooms. Centro da Terra leads with Sara Não Tem Nome’s August residency; a handful of bars in Perdizes and Pinheiros programme midweek sets too. Where: Centro da Terra (Perdizes).

Samba and pagode — Bar Templo carries the Monday torch in the Mooca with Doce Encontro. Where: Bar Templo (Mooca).

Culture — CCBB is open for the MIACENA festival, though its galleries are between exhibitions; most other big museums (MIS, MASP) close on Mondays. Where: CCBB (Centro).

Jazz — Quiet tonight. Blue Note reopens tomorrow and JazzB picks up on Thursday. Where: Blue Note (from Tuesday), JazzB (from Thursday).

Electronic and clubs — Dark. São Paulo’s club scene is a Friday-and-Saturday affair. Where: Barra Funda (weekends).

Pick Your Night

Intimate live music: Sara Não Tem Nome at Centro da Terra in Perdizes — the pick of a quiet Monday.

Samba: Doce Encontro at Bar Templo in the Mooca — a sociable Monday pagode.

Free culture: The MIACENA festival at CCBB São Paulo — open Monday, closed Tuesday.

A quiet drink: A bar in Pinheiros or Vila Madalena — low-key and walkable.

Dance till sunrise: Not on a São Paulo Monday — the clubs are closed.

Where to Go

Centro da Terra — Perdizes A small, intimate room in Perdizes with a reputation for adventurous programming — indie, MPB, experimental and instrumental — and a strong line in Monday-night residencies. Tonight: Sara Não Tem Nome, Não Tem Nome, from 8 pm, with Lorena Hollander, Marina Mole and Vladimir Safatle. Best time: Weeknights for the residencies; the room is best experienced seated and quiet. Cost: R$112 (US$22) is the reference full price, with 40% of tickets released at R$56 (US$11) or less. Sold through Sympla. Address: Rua Piracuama 19, Perdizes Getting there: Metro Sumaré on the green line, about a kilometre on foot, or a short rideshare. The new Perdizes station on line 6 is closer but only runs weekdays 10 am to 3 pm, so it is no use tonight. Good to know: Small room — book ahead, and collect your printed ticket at the box office before the show.

Bar Templo — Mooca A neighbourhood bar in the traditional east-side Mooca, with frequent Monday samba and pagode nights and an unpretentious local crowd. Tonight: Doce Encontro, pagode, doors 8 pm. Over-18s only. Best time: Monday nights when they are on — the Mooca is quiet and residential otherwise. Cost: R$35 (US$7) standing, booked ahead through Clube do Ingresso; tables R$170 (US$33) to R$260 (US$50), some already sold out. Address: Rua Guaimbé 322, Mooca Getting there: Rideshare is easiest; the Mooca is a short ride from the centre. Good to know: A local, low-key spot — come for the atmosphere, and buy your ticket before you travel.

CCBB São Paulo — Centro The Banco do Brasil’s cultural centre in a restored 1901 building — free exhibitions, cinema and theatre, and one of the few big venues open on a Monday. Tonight: The MIACENA performing-arts festival; tonight, a free panel at 5 pm in the theatre. Building open until 8 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm. Closed Tuesdays. Cost: Free, with tickets reserved at bb.com.br/cultura or collected at the box office. Everyone entering the building needs one. Address: Rua Álvares Penteado 112, Centro Histórico Website: ccbb.com.br/sao-paulo Getting there: Metro São Bento (blue line), short walk into the pedestrian centre. Good to know: Centro empties after office hours — use rideshare door-to-door at night.

Planning ahead — reopening this week If tonight feels too quiet, the city’s marquee music rooms are back within a day or two. Casa de Francisca (Sé): Reopens tomorrow, Tuesday 18 August, with two shows at 9:30 pm. Rua Quintino Bocaiúva 22, Sé. Blue Note (Paulista): Back tomorrow — it runs Tuesday to Sunday. Av. Paulista 2073, by Consolação station. JazzB (República): Its jazz programme runs Thursday to Sunday. Rua General Jardim 43. Barra Funda clubs: D-Edge, at Av. Mário de Andrade 141, runs Thursday to Sunday. Good to know: Monday is the quietest night; the city builds from Tuesday.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Perdizes / Pompeia: Leafy and residential, home to Centro da Terra and a scatter of good bars. Calm and walkable.

Mooca: Traditional east-side district with a strong Italian-Brazilian character and a local samba and pagode scene on many Mondays.

Sé / Centro: CCBB and the historic core. Grand by day, very quiet after dark — rideshare door-to-door.

Pinheiros / Vila Madalena: The most reliable spot for a midweek drink, with bars open even on a Monday.

Barra Funda: The club district — dark on a Monday. Come back at the weekend.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

A quiet Monday — the big queer club nights run Friday to Sunday. Tonight, the Frei Caneca and Augusta bars are the easy, mixed, welcoming option.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Tonight’s rooms are all low-key and inclusive; the Augusta corridor keeps a few bars open midweek.

Money & How Paying Works Couvert and cover: Small rooms like Centro da Terra charge a per-person ticket — R$112 (US$22) full price, with 40% of seats at R$56 (US$11) or less. Buy ahead where you can. Cash, card and Pix: Cards and Pix are widely accepted, but carry R$100 (US$20) in cash for smaller east-side bars. Free culture: CCBB is free but everyone needs a ticket, reserved at bb.com.br/cultura or collected at the box office. Tipping: 10% is standard and often added as ‘serviço’. Check before you double-tip.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: The Metrô runs from 4:40 am to midnight, so be on a train by about 12 am — the later times you see posted are arrivals at the end of the line, not departures. On a quiet Monday you’ll likely be home well before then.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and cheap on a Monday, with little surge. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Centro at night: The Sé area is very quiet after dark on a Monday. Stick to lit main roads and rideshare door-to-door.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Perdizes and Pinheiros: Both are calm and residential — easy, safe areas to end a low-key night.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is São Paulo dead on a Monday?

It’s the quietest night, but not dead. Sara Não Tem Nome plays Centro da Terra in Perdizes, Doce Encontro brings pagode to Bar Templo in the Mooca, and CCBB is open in the centre for the MIACENA festival. The clubs and most big music rooms, though, wait for later in the week.

Is CCBB São Paulo open tonight?

Yes — it’s open on Mondays and closed on Tuesdays, running until 8 pm. Entry is free, but everyone needs a ticket. Note the galleries are between exhibitions; what’s on is the MIACENA performing-arts festival, which runs to 22 August.

I’ve just landed at GRU tonight. What can I do?

Be realistic: GRU to Perdizes is 45 to 70 minutes by rideshare, and Centro da Terra needs you to collect a printed ticket before its 8 pm start. Unless you land early, a bar in Pinheiros or Vila Madalena is the easier, walkable option.

What’s the dress code?

Casual everywhere tonight. Comfortable clothes are fine for Centro da Terra, Bar Templo and a Pinheiros bar.

Sources: Ao Vivo (agenda), ccbb.com.br

World.title: ONGC Venezuela License From the US Revives India’s PDVSA Oil Ties
World.content:
Venezuela · Energy

Key Facts — The license ONGC secured a US OFAC license to resume full operations in Venezuela, its finance chief told investors on August 16, 2026.

— The money The clearance lets the Indian firm chase more than US$500 million in dividends frozen inside its Venezuelan ventures.

— The plan ONGC says it now eyes taking over operatorship of projects it currently shares with state producer PDVSA.

— The bigger wave Washington’s General License 50B already covers BP, Chevron, Eni, Maurel & Prom, Repsol and Shell for Venezuelan oil work.

— The limits US rules still bar dealings in Venezuelan debt and bonds, and payments must flow through tightly controlled channels.

India’s oil champion is the newest name in a widening US license wave that has already waved Chevron. Shell, BP, Eni, Repsol and France’s Maurel & Prom back into Venezuela’s fields.

Illustrative photo: an oil tanker carrying petroleum products. India’s ONGC says it won a US OFAC license, disclosed on August 16, 2026, to resume full operations in Venezuela. (Photo: Dennis Cowals, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.)

The ONGC Venezuela license marks India’s return to one of the world’s largest pools of crude. State-owned ONGC says the US Treasury has cleared it to resume full operations in the sanctioned country.

The move could finally unlock hundreds of millions of dollars trapped by years of restrictions.

What the ONGC Venezuela License Actually Permits

The ONGC Venezuela license comes from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, known as OFAC. Since years of sanctions had scared it off, the Indian firm can now run its Venezuelan oil projects normally again.

According to its finance director, the clearance also covers the money side. So the company can finally manage project finances and chase long-frozen earnings.

The Frozen Dividends India Wants Back

For years, ONGC’s Venezuelan profits sat stuck, unable to leave the country. Because banking with Venezuela was choked off, the company could not repatriate a cent.

It now puts the pending dividend at more than US$500 million. Still, getting that cash out will take time and careful, US-approved channels.

Why ONGC Pulled Back in the First Place

ONGC never abandoned Venezuela; instead, it throttled activity to avoid US penalties. Handling Venezuelan oil money had simply become too risky.

As a result, its fields ran below potential while its earnings piled up untouched. Therefore the new license reads as a green light to restart in earnest.

India’s Long Bet on Venezuelan Crude

India’s stake runs through ONGC Videsh, the group’s overseas arm. Since well before the sanctions era, it has co-owned Venezuelan heavy-oil ventures with PDVSA.

Those projects sit in the Orinoco belt, home to some of the planet’s heaviest crude. Meanwhile, for energy-hungry India, the barrels remain a strategic prize worth the long wait.

A Widening US License Wave

ONGC is not acting alone. Meanwhile, Washington has spent 2026 handing out licenses that reopen Venezuela to foreign oil firms.

Its General License 50B names six majors: BP, Chevron, Eni, France’s Maurel & Prom, Repsol and Shell. Although the rules stay strict, each may now run oil and gas operations there.

Chevron and the Companies Already Back In

Chevron leads the pack, since it has held Venezuelan authorizations on and off for years. Today it works under the same broad license as the European majors.

These firms can lift crude, expand fields and sign fresh deals with PDVSA. Even so, every payment must follow channels that Washington controls.

What Washington Still Refuses to Allow

The easing still has clear edges. For example, US rules block trades in Venezuelan debt and bonds, and they bar payment in gold or crypto.

On August 3, 2026, OFAC issued General License 5Y, shielding the disputed PDVSA 2020 bond until September 17. In short, the door is open for oil, not for financiers.

Operatorship: ONGC’s Next Ambition

ONGC is not content to stay a silent partner. Instead, its executives say they may seek operatorship of projects now shared with PDVSA.

Taking the wheel would hand the Indian firm more control over output and costs. Moreover, it would deepen India’s foothold in a recovering oil nation.

What the ONGC Venezuela License Means for Oil Markets

More licensed operators should mean more Venezuelan crude reaching world buyers. So that extra supply matters at a time of jittery global energy prices.

For Venezuela, each returning investor is a lifeline for a battered oil economy. For India, meanwhile, it is a chance to turn a frozen bet into flowing barrels.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ONGC Venezuela license?

It is a US OFAC clearance that lets India’s ONGC resume full oil and gas operations in Venezuela. The company’s finance chief disclosed it to investors on August 16, 2026.

How much money can ONGC recover?

ONGC says more than US$500 million in dividends is frozen inside its Venezuelan projects. The license is meant to help it finally move that cash home.

Which other companies have US licenses for Venezuela?

General License 50B covers BP, Chevron, Eni, France’s Maurel & Prom, Repsol and Shell. Chevron has held Venezuelan authorizations on and off for years.

Is the US lifting all Venezuela sanctions?

No. Washington still bars trading Venezuelan debt and bonds, and it routes oil payments through controlled channels. The easing targets oil operations, not the whole economy.

Sources: The Economic Times; US Treasury (OFAC); Reuters.

World.title: Ecopetrol Data Leak: Hackers Claim 327,095 Files From Colombia’s State Oil Firm
World.content:
Colombia · Business

Key Facts — The claim A ransomware crew called The Gentlemen says it stole 327,095 files, roughly one terabyte, from Ecopetrol and its units.

— The company line Ecopetrol confirms only an unauthorized download tied to about 3,300 user accounts across some 15 group firms.

— The timing Ecopetrol disclosed the incident on July 17, 2026, and the hackers claimed responsibility a day later.

— The response Ecopetrol says it blocked the ransomware encryption, revoked access, and reported the case to Colombia’s Attorney General.

— The impact The company reports no disruption to oil production, and it says user passwords were not captured.

Colombia’s biggest company confirms a breach of some 3,300 accounts, yet insists no passwords fell and no oil stopped flowing.

Illustrative photo: a monument at an Ecopetrol site in Colombia. Ecopetrol disclosed the cyberattack on July 17, 2026, and confirmed a breach tied to about 3,300 accounts. (Photo: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The Ecopetrol data leak has become a public standoff between Colombia’s state oil giant and the hackers who hit it. A group calling itself The Gentlemen says it walked off with 327,095 files.

Ecopetrol, however, insists the real breach was far narrower than that.

What the hackers say they took

A ransomware group known as The Gentlemen went public a day after Ecopetrol’s disclosure. It claimed to hold up to one terabyte of company data.

In its telling, that haul spans Ecopetrol itself and a string of subsidiaries. So far, though, those boasts rest on the attackers’ own word, not the company’s.

What Ecopetrol actually confirms

Ecopetrol’s official account is much narrower. It confirms an unauthorized download of data tied to roughly 3,300 user accounts.

Those accounts sat in cloud file storage across about 15 companies in the Ecopetrol group. Beyond that, the firm has not put a total file count or data volume on the record.

The Exploration and Production segment engages in the exploration and production of oil and gas. The Transport and Logistics segment is involved in…

The 327,095-file number, explained

The headline figure of 327,095 files is a hacker claim, not a company confirmation. It surfaced through Colombian media, including a Caracol Radio analysis of the breach.

El País reported the same order of magnitude, describing more than 327,000 files and up to a terabyte. Still, Ecopetrol has not validated any such count.

Inside the Ecopetrol data leak

The Ecopetrol data leak is not just a threat on paper. By late July, an external actor had published material copied from 15 group companies, the firm told regulators.

According to El País, the attackers claim the trove includes drilling records for fields such as Rubiales and Casabe. They also allege it holds payroll, banking, medical and biometric details on staff.

A clash over stolen passwords

The most pointed dispute is over credentials. The Gentlemen say they grabbed active VPN and FortiClient logins, plus password-vault contents.

Ecopetrol flatly denies it. The company says user identities were not exposed and that no access credentials were captured.

How Ecopetrol responded

Ecopetrol says its defenses blocked the encryption phase of the attack before files could be locked. As a result, the ransomware never fully detonated.

The company then revoked the intruder’s access and throttled mass downloads. Meanwhile, it filed a criminal complaint with Colombia’s Attorney General and looped in national cyber agencies.

Was oil production affected?

This is the reassuring part of the story, at least for now. Ecopetrol reports no material disruption to its operations, production capacity or essential services.

Because the breach hit office cloud storage rather than industrial controls, the pumps kept running. In short, this reads as a data theft, not a shutdown of the oil business.

The extortion and the deadline

Ecopetrol confirms the attacker made extortion demands and threatened to publish the stolen files. When those threats were ignored, the data began appearing online.

Caracol Radio, citing prosecutors, reported a blunt ultimatum: behave, or the material goes public in seven days. Even so, no specific ransom amount has been confirmed publicly.

Why this matters for Colombia

Ecopetrol is not just any target. It is Colombia’s largest company and a pillar of the national budget, so an attack on it lands as a public-interest event.

The episode also lands during a tense stretch for the firm’s leadership and regulators. For a foreign reader, it is a reminder that Latin America’s biggest firms now face the same ransomware pressure as Western ones.

What to watch next

The open question is how much of the hackers’ claim proves real. Investigators must still weigh the 327,095-file boast against what Ecopetrol will admit.

The company is working with authorities to pull the leaked material offline. Yet once files reach the dark web, they rarely disappear for good.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who attacked Ecopetrol?

A ransomware group calling itself The Gentlemen claimed responsibility. Ecopetrol officially describes the attacker only as an unidentified external actor.

Is the 327,095-files figure confirmed?

No. It is a claim made by the hackers and relayed by Colombian media. Ecopetrol has confirmed only an unauthorized download tied to about 3,300 accounts.

Did the attack stop Ecopetrol’s oil production?

Ecopetrol says no. It reports no material disruption to operations, production or essential services, because the breach hit cloud file storage rather than industrial systems.

When did this happen?

Ecopetrol disclosed the incident on July 17, 2026. The Gentlemen claimed the attack a day later, and data was published online by late July.

Sources: Reuters; El País; TechRadar; Caracol Radio.

World.title: Mexico’s Top Court Backs ISSSTE Pension Fund Boosting State Workers Up to US$1,050 a Month
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts — The ruling On August 12, 2026, Mexico’s Supreme Court unanimously upheld the 2024 law that created the Fondo de Pensiones para el Bienestar (Well-Being Pension Fund).

— The mechanism The fund tops up low individual-account pensions toward a worker’s final salary, but only up to a monthly ceiling.

— The cap For 2026 that ceiling is 17,885.85 pesos a month, roughly US$1,050 at 17.01 pesos per dollar (August 17, 2026).

— The age decree A separate June 24, 2025 decree lowers ISSSTE retirement ages for one older group, from 56 and 58 today toward 53 and 55 by 2034.

— The caveat President Claudia Sheinbaum has said the 2007 reform cannot be fully reversed because the money is not there.

The ruling clears the legal cloud over a pension top-up fund. Even as viral posts wildly overstate what state workers will actually receive.

Illustrative photo: Mexico’s Supreme Court in Mexico City, which on August 12, 2026 upheld the 2024 law creating the Well-Being Pension Fund. (Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Mexico’s Supreme Court has cleared the biggest legal question hanging over the country’s new ISSSTE pension safety net for government workers. On August 12, 2026.

The justices unanimously upheld the 2024 law that created a fund to lift meager retirement checks toward a worker’s final paycheck. The decision settles the fund’s future, yet it also exposes how far online claims about the policy have drifted from the facts.

What Mexico’s Top Court Decided

On August 12, 2026, the Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nacion resolved a challenge known as Accion de Inconstitucionalidad 116/2024. By a unanimous vote, it declared the 2024 reforms that built the Well-Being Pension Fund constitutional.

The court also clarified an important point for savers. Workers keep ownership of their individual retirement accounts, and they can reclaim those funds at any time.

Even after balances are transferred into the new pool.

How the ISSSTE Pension Top-Up Actually Works

The core idea is a complement, not a giveaway. Because individual accounts often replace only a fraction of a final salary.

The fund pays the difference to bring a pension closer to 100% of that last wage. Still, the help is bounded.

It applies to workers under the individual-account systems created for private-sector staff in 1997 and for state workers in 2007. And it stops at a fixed monthly ceiling.

The Money, in Plain Numbers

The ceiling tracks the average registered wage at Mexico’s social security institute, updated each January for inflation. It started at 16,777.68 pesos in 2024 and rose to 17,364.90 pesos in 2025.

For 2026 the cap is 17,885.85 pesos a month, about US$1,050 at 17.01 pesos per dollar on August 17, 2026. Reputable Mexican coverage has put the typical top-up much lower, near 3,975 pesos.

So most beneficiaries receive far less than the headline ceiling.

The Retirement-Age Rollback

A separate move sits alongside the fund. A decree published in the official gazette on June 24.

2025 reforms the ISSSTE law’s Tenth Transitory article, which governs an older cohort of state workers. As a result, the minimum retirement age freezes and then falls in stages.

Women drop from 56 today toward 53 by 2034, while men move from 58 toward 55. Reversing the age increases the 2007 reform had set in motion for that group.

Who Actually Benefits

The two measures reach different people. The age rollback covers the Tenth Transitory group, longtime state employees who joined before 2007 and stayed in the old defined-benefit scheme.

Analysts estimate roughly 968,000 workers, though that figure is not stated in the decree itself. Meanwhile, the fund’s top-up targets those on individual accounts.

That includes 1997-era private-sector workers and post-2007 ISSSTE staff whose savings alone would deliver a thin pension.

What This Is Not: The Viral Claims

Social posts and content farms have described the policy as an automatic 14,700-peso monthly raise and a 340% jump for millions. Those exact figures do not appear in the official decrees.

The social security institute’s own materials, or major outlets such as Reuters and La Jornada. In fact, they read as dramatized extrapolations from the cap.

The real design is a capped complement plus an age change for one cohort, not a flat cash bonus paid to everyone.

Why Sheinbaum Says She Cannot Go Further

President Claudia Sheinbaum has been blunt about the limits. She has said Mexico cannot return to the pre-2007 ISSSTE rules because the public resources simply are not there.

So the strategy is repair rather than repeal. The government layers a solidarity top-up and an earlier retirement age onto the existing system.

Instead of tearing up the 1997 and 2007 laws.

The 2007 Reform, Briefly

The 2007 overhaul moved new state workers onto personal savings accounts, much like Chile’s model and Mexico’s own 1997 private-sector shift. The promise was fiscal stability; the trade-off was smaller, market-linked pensions.

Two decades on, many of those pensions look too small to live on. That gap is exactly what the new fund tries to close, at least up to its ceiling.

What Happens Next

With the court challenge resolved, the fund can keep operating without a constitutional cloud overhead. Its ceiling will continue to rise each January in line with inflation.

For workers, the practical takeaway is simple. Check which regime you fall under, because the age decree and the top-up reach separate groups.

And neither delivers the eye-popping numbers circulating online.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Sheinbaum reverse Mexico’s 2007 ISSSTE pension reform?

Not fully. A June 2025 decree rolls back retirement-age increases for one older cohort.

How much is the ISSSTE pension top-up worth?

The complement lifts a pension toward the worker’s final salary, capped at 17,885.85 pesos a month in 2026, about US$1,050. Reputable reporting suggests the average actual top-up is far smaller, near 3,975 pesos.

Is the 14,700-peso raise or 340% increase real?

Those figures circulate on content farms and social media, not in the official decrees or major news outlets. They appear to be extrapolations from the fund’s cap rather than a guaranteed payment.

What did the Supreme Court decide on August 12, 2026?

It unanimously upheld the 2024 law creating the Well-Being Pension Fund and confirmed that workers keep ownership of their individual accounts and can reclaim the money.

Sources: Diario Oficial de la Federacion; Aristegui Noticias; La Jornada; IMSS; Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nacion.

World.title: Costa Rica Under Orange Alert as Caribbean Ground Reaches Saturation
World.content:
The ground across the Caribbean can no longer absorb water. Soil saturation in Caribbean river basins sits between 90 and 100%, according to the Instituto Meteorológico Nacional, and basins in the South Pacific are above 85%. Everything that falls today runs off, which is why Costa Rica woke up under an orange alert.

If you are in the Caribbean, the Northern Zone or Turrialba, treat today as a day to change plans rather than push through them. Those areas carry the orange alert. The Central Valley, Central Pacific and South Pacific are on yellow. The North Pacific has no alert at all, so Guanacaste is not part of this.

Orange is one step below the highest level, and it is not a prediction. It means damage is already happening, which is why shelters and evacuations came before the alert rather than after it. The rain has been heavy overnight. In the six hours to 4 a.m., Puerto Viejo de Sarapiquí took 59.6 millimeters (2.3 inches) and Canta Bratsi in the South Caribbean took 57.3 millimeters (2.3 inches). The strongest gust recorded was 52 kilometers per hour (32 miles per hour) at Asada Guayabo.

More is coming, and the system driving it has not arrived yet. Tropical wave No. 33 was still sitting near the Panama border when the meteorological institute issued its 4:07 a.m. bulletin. It crosses the country during the day, on top of ground that is already at capacity.

Expect 20 to 50 millimetres (0.8 to 2 inches) over 12 hours in the Caribbean and Northern Zone, with peaks that could pass 90 millimetres (3.5 inches). The North Pacific and Central Valley are looking at 10 to 50 millimetres (0.4 to 2 inches). The Central and South Pacific get downpours with thunderstorms, generally 10 to 20 millimetres (0.4 to 0.8 inches) but with peaks to 50 millimetres (2 inches).

Trade winds stay moderate with occasional strong gusts in mountain areas, running 60 to 80 kilometres per hour (37 to 50 miles per hour). In isolated cases near storm clouds, gusts can reach 100 kilometres per hour (62 miles per hour). That is enough to bring down branches and power lines, so if you feel a sudden strong gust near a storm cloud, get indoors rather than waiting to see what happens.

Two travel warnings in this bulletin matter if you have anything booked. Pilots are advised to expect increased turbulence, so a bumpy approach into San José or Liberia today is normal rather than alarming. And sea conditions are rougher, particularly in the southern part of the North Pacific, the Gulf of Nicoya and the Central and South Pacific. If you have a boat tour, a Nicoya crossing or a Tortuguero transfer, call the operator this morning instead of assuming it sails.

There is a warning for towns too. Urban drainage systems may not cope with the volume, which means streets flood in places that are nowhere near a river. If you live or are staying somewhere that has puddled badly before, that is your indicator. The weekend already displaced people. At least 495 were in shelters as of Sunday evening, with 154 across three sites in the Caribbean, 331 across seven sites in Sarapiquí and 10 in Turrialba. The community of Ulima de Florencia was left almost entirely underwater.

Several communities in Talamanca are cut off as the Sixaola river runs high, and homes have taken damage in Valle de La Estrella, Siquirres, Guácimo and Matina. In Sarapiquí the Tigre river has left its channel, and the Sarapiquí, Puerto Viejo and Sucio rivers are being watched.

Roads are the part most likely to change while you are reading this. Route 32 to Limón stayed closed overnight because the saturated slopes at Cerro Zurquí were still judged too likely to give way, and an inspection was scheduled for this morning. Route 230 between Cot and Turrialba has slide damage, and the section of Route 415 between Turrialba and La Herediana known locally as the sinkhole remains closed. Check the current status before you drive rather than relying on this or any other article.

Classes are cancelled at 934 schools, with all campuses closed across the Turrialba, Sarapiquí, Limón and Sulá regional directorates. The single most useful habit today is refusing to drive through standing water. You cannot see whether the road underneath is still there, and moving water needs surprisingly little depth to lift a vehicle off its wheels.

The second is giving hillsides room on mountain routes, especially where you can see fresh mud or fallen material at the pavement edge, because that means the slope is still moving. The meteorological institute issues its next bulletin at 10 a.m.

World.title: Costa Rican Surfers Chase a Home Title as WSL Finals Day Runs at Playa Hermosa
World.content:
Professional surfing’s return to Costa Rica reaches its decisive stage today, with the quarterfinals, semifinals and final of the Garabito Surf City Pro all set to run in a single session at Playa Hermosa, on the Central Pacific coast. The World Surf League set the first call for 6:30 a.m. Four quarterfinal heats, two semifinals and one final remain to be decided in each division. Competition sat on standby through much of Saturday before the closing rounds were pushed to Sunday.

Leilani McGonagle took the strongest Costa Rican result into finals day. The Olympian and Championship Tour wildcard came through the round of 16 on Saturday with the most convincing win of the round in the women’s draw, keeping alive the prospect of a home victory at the first World Surf League Qualifying Series event staged in the country since 2018.

The men’s draw arrives at the quarterfinals with several in-form international contenders. Jett Schilling posted a 15.40 ride and a 16.00 heat total in the round of 32, among the highest scores of the event. Lucas Cassity and Blayr Barton also advanced through Saturday’s rounds.

Costa Rica entered a large contingent, led by Carlos “Cali” Muñoz, Sam Reidy, Darshan Antequera, Noe Mar McGonagle, Jairo Pérez and Malakai Martínez. Muñoz won the last World Surf League event held in the country, the Essential Costa Rica Surf Pro at Jacó in October 2018, when Germany’s Rachel Presti took the women’s title.

The competition carries a QS 2,000 rating, meaning the winners collect up to 2,000 ranking points toward Challenger Series qualification, the tier immediately below the Championship Tour. Weather remains a factor. The Instituto Meteorológico Nacional forecast afternoon showers and thunderstorms for the Central and South Pacific on Sunday, with activity reaching coastal sectors by evening.

The Comisión Nacional de Emergencias has the Central Pacific under a green alert as unstable conditions continue. For Garabito, the event doubles as a tourism showcase. The Instituto Costarricense de Turismo (ICT) reports that more than 2.6 million tourists arrive by air each year and that roughly 17 percent surf on Pacific or Caribbean beaches, with as many as 600,000 surfers visiting in a single year. Playa Hermosa, just south of Jacó, is known for powerful and consistent beach breaks better suited to experienced surfers than to beginners.

The closing rounds are being broadcast live on worldsurfleague.com and through the free World Surf League app. Heats run back to back once the event is called on, so the timing of the final depends on how the surf holds up through the day.

World.title: Costa Rica Heavy Rains Cause Flooding and Travel Disruptions
World.content:
Heavy rains from Tropical Wave No. 32 left flooding, overflowing rivers, landslides and road problems across several parts of Costa Rica, while forecasters warned that unstable conditions would continue Sunday. The Caribbean and Northern Zone are expected to receive the heaviest rainfall, with moderate to strong showers possible through the morning. Rain and thunderstorms are also forecast for parts of the Pacific and Central Valley later in the day.

The weekend weather has already caused problems in Cartago, Limón and Alajuela. Turrialba was among the hardest-hit areas Saturday after heavy rainfall caused the Turrialba River to rise sharply. One house fell into the river, while other homes were affected and residents in the immediate area were warned not to return because of unstable conditions.

A landslide was also reported in San Rafael de Santa Cruz de Turrialba, affecting elderly residents. Authorities closed the Las Monjas bridge in central Turrialba as a precaution after the river current apparently damaged part of its foundation. Elsewhere in Cartago province, a landslide blocked National Route 10 in the Quebrada Honda area near Juan Viñas, while flooding affected roads in Santa Teresita de Turrialba and Río Bajo de Abarca in Alvarado.

Those heading through mountainous parts of Cartago should check road conditions before leaving, particularly on routes toward Turrialba and Irazú Volcano.Along Route 219 toward Irazú Volcano National Park, rain caused additional road damage and difficult driving conditions.

The weather also caused trouble on Route 32, the main highway between San José and Limón. A landslide closed the highway for approximately four hours Saturday before crews removed debris and reopened the road. In Matina, Limón province, flooding was reported in the Davao area. An emergency shelter was prepared in the nearby community of Larga Distancia as a precaution, although no residents had been moved there at the time of the latest report.

Farther north, overflowing rivers affected San Juan and Pataste in Guatuso, Alajuela. Police officers were sent through affected communities to determine whether families needed assistance. The risk has not ended with the passage of the tropical wave. Costa Rica remains under the influence of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, while strong trade winds continue to bring moisture from the Caribbean. Those conditions are expected to keep the atmosphere unstable Sunday.

The Caribbean and Northern Zone face the greatest risk this morning, with recurring moderate to heavy rainfall possible. The Pacific Central and South are expected to see scattered afternoon downpours and thunderstorms, while the Central Valley could experience periods of rain and isolated showers.

Strong winds are yet another concern. Gusts could reach 40 to 60 km/h (25 to 37 mph) in lower areas and 70 to 90 km/h (43 to 56 mph) in mountainous locations. The combination of additional rainfall and already saturated ground increases the possibility of new landslides, flash flooding and rising rivers. Soil saturation in mountainous Caribbean watersheds is estimated at between 70% and 100%, while areas around the Golfo Dulce in southern Costa Rica are above 90%.

The Northern Zone and Caribbean remain under a yellow weather alert, while the Central Valley and the Central and South Pacific are under a lower-level green alert. Residents and visitors traveling Sunday are advised to use additional caution around rivers, steep slopes and roads with a history of landslides. Conditions can change quickly during heavy rain, particularly on mountain highways.

Anyone driving today should also confirm road conditions before heading toward Limón, Turrialba or other areas affected by yesterday’s storms.

World.title: Costa Rica Beach Overwhelmed by Trash Flowing Down Tárcoles River
World.content:
A Pacific beach with the potential to attract tourists has instead become one of the clearest examples of Costa Rica’s struggle with waste, as garbage carried down the Tárcoles River continues to wash ashore at Guacalillo Beach. About 90 minutes from San José, Guacalillo sits near the mouth of the Tárcoles, where waste carried from the Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA) reaches the Pacific Ocean.

Plastic bottles, pieces of cardboard, glass and other household garbage collect along the sand and surrounding vegetation. Volunteers have also encountered syringes, shoe soles, cosmetics, utensils and other discarded objects. Much of the problem begins far from the coast. Garbage discarded improperly in the Central Valley can enter streams and rivers that eventually feed into the Tárcoles.

The river then carries the waste west toward Puntarenas, where currents and tides deposit part of it along Guacalillo and nearby beaches. The result is a frustrating cycle for both those who live there and environmental groups. Volunteers remove bags of garbage, only for new debris to arrive with the river, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall.

Community members and organizations now have cleanup efforts at least every weekend, spending hours collecting and separating waste from the sand, driftwood and vegetation. The contamination presents an especially difficult challenge for a community that would like Guacalillo to become better known as a tourism destination. Instead of beachgoers, stretches of shoreline can be dominated by accumulated trash and scavenging birds.

There are now efforts to build a more permanent response. At the end of July, Guacalillo opened Puntarenas province’s first Beach Cleanup and Volunteer Center, designed to support waste collection, environmental education and organized volunteer work. The facility was developed in response to the persistent amount of garbage reaching the area through the Tárcoles.

The center includes areas for training and volunteer activities, as well as a native-plant nursery for reforestation, a plastic museum intended to promote environmental education and a protected area for sea turtle eggs from turtles nesting along the beach. Organizers also hope to recover materials that can still be reused while finding alternatives for harder-to-process waste. Some plastics can be recovered, while materials such as tires and textiles may potentially be transformed for use in asphalt or construction materials.

The scale of the broader waste problem, however, remains significant. Costa Rica generates about 4,000 metric tons of solid waste each day, while only about 13% is recycled. An estimate for 2022 found that households generated more than 229,000 metric tons of plastic waste, with hundreds of tons reaching aquatic environments and tens of thousands of tons affecting land ecosystems.

For Guacalillo, that national problem becomes visible on the sand. The beach’s location makes it particularly vulnerable because it effectively sits at the end of a drainage system serving a large portion of the country’s most densely populated region. Cleaning the shoreline can improve conditions temporarily, but it does not stop more garbage from moving downstream.

That means residents and volunteers are fighting the problem at its final destination rather than at its source. Still, the community sees environmental recovery as part of Guacalillo’s economic future. The new center is intended not only to organize cleanups but also to create opportunities for local families, environmental education and sustainable tourism.

For now, volunteers continue returning to the beach, picking up bottles, plastic, shoes, syringes and countless other reminders of a pollution problem that began many kilometers upstream.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Route 32 Reopens After a Morning Landslide Shuts the Highway
World.content:
If you are driving to the Caribbean today, Route 32 is open. It was not open this morning, and the conditions that closed it have not gone anywhere. The Ministry of Public Works and Transportation shut the highway shortly after 9 a.m. this morning, when material came down onto the road. Crews cleared it and the ministry restored traffic at 1:39 p.m., about four hours later.

No reopening time was given while the road was shut. That is standard, and it is not the authorities being cagey with you. Nobody can estimate a reopening until crews reach the site, see how much material came down and confirm the slope above it has stopped moving.

If the next closure catches you, you have three ways around. Route 10, between Siquirres and Turrialba, takes any vehicle. So does the Bajos de Chilamate-Vuelta de Kooper corridor. Vara Blanca is open to light vehicles only, so leave the loaded pickup and the heavy SUV off it.

All three add real time to the trip, and all three get crowded fast when Route 32 goes down. Build in the extra hours before you leave rather than discovering them at the Zurquí backup. The reason this keeps happening sits in the terrain. Route 32 climbs through Braulio Carrillo National Park on a stretch cut between steep, forested slopes, and the ground there has been saturated for weeks.

Once soil is that wet, it stops absorbing rain and starts sliding. It does not take a downpour to bring rock, mud and whole trees onto the lanes. A moderate shower on already-soaked ground will do it.

That is exactly the pattern today. Tropical Wave No. 32 crossed the country this morning with the Intertropical Convergence Zone sitting overhead, and the Caribbean slope and Northern Zone are under a yellow alert because of it. Six-hour rainfall totals of 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) were forecast for the region, with localized peaks near 75 millimeters (3 inches) in the mountains.

So check the road right before you leave, not the night before. A highway that reopens at lunchtime can be shut again by dinner, and the status you saw yesterday tells you almost nothing about the status now.

Road updates go out on the ministry’s social media as they happen rather than on a fixed schedule, which is worth knowing if you are used to checking a website and assuming silence means the road is fine. Today’s closure also landed on a holiday. Saturday is Mother’s Day, a mandatory-pay national holiday, which puts far more cars on the road than an ordinary weekend and makes every alternate route slower than the map suggests.

This is at least the second time this month the highway has been cut. It closed on the evening of August 5 and stayed shut into the following morning, and it went down repeatedly in July during the flooding that followed Tropical Wave No. 24.

Route 32 is the only fast link between the Central Valley and Limón, and it carries commuters, tour buses and the freight moving to and from the ports at Moín. When it shuts, the cost lands on everyone at once, which is why a four-hour closure counts as a good outcome here.

Green season runs to November, and the slopes above this road will keep giving way until the ground dries out. The realistic answer is not to avoid the Caribbean but to treat the drive as something to time rather than assume.

World.title: Belize, Guatemala and Mexico mark first Anniversary of Calakmul Declaration
World.content:
Belize, Guatemala and Mexico mark first Anniversary of Calakmul Declaration

By Zoila Palma: Belize, Guatemala and Mexico have marked the first anniversary of the Calakmul Declaration, a regional commitment to safeguard the Great Selva Maya and strengthen cooperation on biodiversity and conservation.

The milestone was commemorated at the Caracol Archaeological Reserve, where the Institute of Archaeology joined wildlife and natural resource conservation organizations.

The European Union in Belize also joined regional partners to recognize the anniversary, with EU Ambassador Dr. Erja Askola and EU Ambassador to Guatemala Johanna Karanko participating alongside government representatives, civil society organizations and other stakeholders.

The EU described the declaration as an important milestone for biodiversity protection and conservation efforts across the region.

The Selva Maya is considered one of the most critical ecosystems in the Americas, covering approximately 5.7 million hectares of forest across Belize, Guatemala and Mexico.

Regional cooperation is considered essential to protecting the forest while promoting sustainable development and supporting communities and local economies in the three countries.

The European Union said it has provided significant financial support through various programmes aimed at preserving and protecting the Selva Maya.

World.title: Armed men tie up Northern Fisherman security guard during early-morning burglary
World.content:
Armed men tie up Northern Fisherman security guard during early-morning burglary

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an aggravated burglary at the Northern Fisherman Cooperative in Belize City where a security guard was allegedly held at gunpoint and tied up by a group of masked men early Saturday morning.

According to police, a security guard reported that at around 2:00 a.m. on August 15, he was performing security duties at Northern Fisheries when approximately four masked men, each reportedly armed with a firearm, approached him.

The gunmen allegedly pointed their weapons at him and ordered him not to move before tying him up and placing him on the ground.

The guard told investigators that about 20 minutes later, he heard the intruders say they had found a chest inside one of the offices. He then reportedly heard what sounded like a metal object being dragged from the building before hearing a vehicle speed away.

Police visited and processed the scene and observed surveillance cameras mounted around the building. Investigators are reportedly still working to determine exactly what was stolen.

No arrests have been reported and the investigation continues.

World.title: Canadian man who ran from police for drinking in public busted with 6.78 grams of cocaine; charged with drug trafficking
World.content:
Canadian man who ran from police for drinking in public busted with 6.78 grams of cocaine; charged with drug trafficking

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Canadian businessman living in Placencia has been charged with two counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply after police allegedly found a total of 6.78 grams of suspected cocaine in his possession on Sunday evening.

Police say that at about 6:45 p.m. on August 16, officers were conducting mobile patrol on the Placencia Main Road when their attention was drawn to 52-year-old Grant Arthur Stowell, who was allegedly drinking from a Belikin beer bottle in public.

According to police, when officers approached and asked Stowell to desist from public drinking, he became agitated and eventually ran into a nearby store. An officer pursued him and allegedly saw Stowell remove an item from his pocket and place it on a store shelf.

Police retrieved a piece of tissue paper which allegedly contained a small transparent plastic bag with a white powdery substance suspected to be cocaine. The substance was later weighed at 5.60 grams.

Police say a subsequent search of Stowell’s wallet led to the discovery of another small plastic bag containing suspected cocaine weighing 1.18 grams.

Stowell, described by police as a Canadian business owner residing in Placencia, was formally arrested and charged with two counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply. He reportedly exercised his right to remain silent after being cautioned.

World.title: Belize advances Regional Environmental action with new strategies and partnerships
World.content:
Belize advances Regional Environmental action with new strategies and partnerships

By Zoila Palma: Belize has marked several important milestones in regional environmental action with the launch of major initiatives aimed at protecting natural resources, strengthening climate resilience and promoting sustainable development.

The initiatives were launched by the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management in collaboration with the Central American Commission on Environment and Development (CCAD) during Belize’s Pro Tempore Presidency.

Among the key developments is the updated CCAD Regional Environmental Framework Strategy (ERAM) 2026–2035, which will serve as a shared environmental strategy for the SICA region.

The framework seeks to promote an environmentally sustainable, resilient and inclusive future through action on environmental quality, seas and biodiversity, integrated water-resource management, forests and sustainable landscapes, and climate change.

Belize also joined the launch of the new “Great Forests of Central America and the Dominican Republic” brand, known as Green Heritage or “Patrimonio Verde.”

The communication strategy aims to strengthen regional storytelling by highlighting measurable results, environmental impacts, data-driven decision-making and the network of partners working across Central America and the Dominican Republic.

Another major initiative is the regional CAM Project, implemented in partnership with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), which will invest US$20 million to improve watershed management and protect marine ecosystems.

Belize’s Belize River, New River and Rio Hondo watersheds have been identified as priority areas.

Chief Environmental Officer Anthony Mai said the project will strengthen governance, promote integrated watershed and coastal-zone management, support nature-based solutions and sustainable financing, and build regional technical capacity.

Belize also formalized a new Memorandum of Understanding with The Nature Conservancy to strengthen cooperation on freshwater conservation and aquatic ecosystem management.

The partnership will support ecosystem restoration, monitoring and data systems, freshwater biodiversity conservation, climate adaptation, public awareness and transboundary water cooperation.

The initiatives were supported by Minister Orlando Habet, CEO Milagro Matus and technical leaders from the Ministry and regional partners, as Belize continues efforts toward a more resilient and sustainable future.

World.title: Belize Police Department honors retired officers from Southern Region
World.content:
Belize Police Department honors retired officers from Southern Region

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department hosted a luncheon on Saturday, August 15, 2026, to honor retired police officers from the Southern Region and recognize their years of dedicated service to the Department and the people of Belize.

Held from 10:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., the luncheon provided an opportunity for retired officers to reconnect with former colleagues, share memories and celebrate the lasting bonds formed during their years of service within the Belize Police Department.

The retirees expressed their appreciation for the recognition and extended special thanks to Minister of Home Affairs Julius Espat and Commissioner of Police Richard Rosado.

The Belize Police Department said it proudly salutes its retired officers, emphasizing that their service continues to matter and their legacy remains part of the institution.

World.title: International News: Colombian President asks Trump to suspend tariffs as earthquake recovery efforts continue
World.content:
International News: Colombian President asks Trump to suspend tariffs as earthquake recovery efforts continue

By Zoila Palma: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has asked U.S. President Donald Trump to temporarily suspend tariffs on Colombian products as the South American nation struggles to recover from a powerful earthquake that has killed at least 289 people.

De la Espriella, who took office earlier this month, said the tariff relief would help businesses affected by the disaster.

The president said he spoke with Trump on Saturday and thanked him for U.S. assistance following the 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

He said he asked the U.S. leader to consider temporarily suspending the tariffs to provide relief to Colombian businesses facing difficult economic conditions following the disaster.

The Trump administration had not immediately responded to the request, AP reports.

The United States has committed $26.5 million in emergency assistance, including food, shelter and medical supplies, according to the U.S. State Department.

The earthquake struck western Colombia last Monday, severely affecting cities including Pereira, Cali and Quibdó, with communities along the Pacific coast suffering some of the heaviest damage. The government has declared the disaster a national emergency.

World.title: International News: Mexico and U.S. seek to restore security cooperation despite visa dispute
World.content:
International News: Mexico and U.S. seek to restore security cooperation despite visa dispute

By Zoila Palma: Mexico and the United States are working to maintain and strengthen security cooperation despite a growing diplomatic dispute over the revoked U.S. visa of Andy López Beltrán, son of former Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson announced a new agreement allowing Mexico access to the U.S. market for drone procurement, while Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch is set to attend a major U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) conference in Argentina.

The visa dispute escalated after López Beltrán accused the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump of revoking his entry permit for political reasons.

He denied any wrongdoing and described the decision as politically motivated. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended López Beltrán, saying there is no evidence against him, while members of the ruling Morena party have rallied behind the former president’s son and described the U.S. action as interference in Mexico’s sovereignty.

Despite the tensions, officials on both sides continue to emphasize cooperation on security matters.

U.S. officials have highlighted joint efforts, while the U.S. Embassy in Mexico stated that visas can be cancelled when there are reasons to do so, regardless of the holder’s political views. The embassy also highlighted a photograph of Johnson and García Harfuch, saying the two countries are delivering results on priority issues under the leadership of Trump and Sheinbaum.

García Harfuch’s decision to attend the International Conference on Drug Control in Argentina is being viewed as another sign that both governments are seeking to keep security cooperation moving forward.

World.title: Belmopan Aggregates and Hardware becomes Troy-Bilt riding mower supplier
World.content:
Belmopan Aggregates and Hardware becomes Troy-Bilt riding mower supplier

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The push mower has met its upgrade. Belmopan Aggregates and Hardware is now a supplier of Troy-Bilt riding lawn mowers, bringing the American brand’s ride-on machines, built for life, as the company’s slogan goes, to Belizean lawns.

The lineup on offer includes traditional lawn tractors and the zero-turn Z42, the class of machine that turns on its own axis to cut cleanly around trees, fence posts and flower beds without the back-and-forth of conventional mowers.

The audience is anyone for whom grass is measured in acres rather than square feet: large residential compounds, schools and churches, resorts, sporting grounds and the landscaping crews that maintain them. In rainy season, when grass regrows in days, a riding mower turns a punishing weekly chore into an hour in a seat, and for commercial cutters, speed is income.

BAH, the capital’s hardware stalwart since 1990, backs the machines with its established parts and service relationships.

Troy-Bilt riding mowers are available at 5 Forest Drive, Belmopan. WhatsApp 610-0715, call 822-3715, or email [email protected] for models and pricing.

World.title: Defend truth, liberty
World.content:
Reverend Astor Carlyle (right) shakes hands with Governor General Sir Patrick Allen as Lady Allen (second right) and Chief of Defence Staff Vice Admiral Antonette Wemyss Gorman (left) look on at the end of Sunday’s church service commemorating 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension, Up Park Camp in St Andrew. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Jamaicans have been urged to summon the courage of a previous generation and stand firm in defence of truth and liberty just as men and women from this region answered the call to serve when World War II plunged the world into geopolitical turmoil and economic uncertainty.



Reverend Captain Astor Carlyle made the appeal on Sunday in his sermon during the service celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Royal Air Forces Association (RAFA) Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension inside the Jamaica Defence Force’s Up Park Camp headquarters in St Andrew.

According to RAFA, the service, held under the theme ‘80 years of service, sacrifice, and unity’, marks the commencement of a year of celebrations to mark its founding.

Referencing the first lesson — Isaiah 6:1-8, which tells of the prophet Isaiah seeing a vision of God, realising he is sinful, gets cleansed by a burning coal, and volunteers to serve God by saying, ‘Here am I. Send me!’ — Rev Carlyle said that in the time of Isaiah, Judah needed someone to shoulder the responsibility of being God’s representative during great confusion.

“Throughout the Bible, God asks questions, but there is one question from the lips of God that is very relevant for a day like this when we celebrate 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association; it is a question that we heard in the first scripture reading today: Whom shall I send? Who will go for us? And this was a question asked of the prophet Isaiah in a time that needed a Godly voice and a Godly presence to bring calm and consciousness to a nation in crisis,” Carlyle told the congregation of mostly ex-servicemen and women.

“This was a time of chaos, a time of complexity, a time of corruption, and when the young Isaiah stood in the presence of God and considered the grave need, he responded with five words, ‘Here am I, send me.’ Isaiah saw what was at stake, and without concern for himself, he answered in the affirmative,” Carlyle said.

“This is a picture of the kind of spirit with which our Caribbean service members engaged the desperate call from the allied forces in 1939. It was a time of geopolitical and economic instability. Dictators were emerging in Europe and Asia, threatening the fragile peace that the Treaty of Versailles sought to ensure. The Great Depression and the subsequent invasion of Poland required the allied forces to sound the rallying call, and with a spirit of duty and a sense of mission our Caribbean servicemen said ‘Here am I, send me.’ Some trained as pilots, some trained as navigators, some were ground crew under the British Commonwealth air training plan.

“They served in Europe, they served in North Africa, they served in the Mediterranean, they served in Asia. Many Jamaicans served with the Royal Air Force bomber command and fighter command, defending Britain during air raids and helping push back the Axis forces. These young men of the Caribbean faced grave danger, but not for fame or reward, they believed in freedom that was worth defending and they paid the ultimate sacrifice. That is why we celebrate their gallantry today,” Carlyle said.

He stated that the service Jamaicans gave during the war stands as a reminder that the call to duty is for the willing, and encouraged citizens to demonstrate a willingness to serve, just as the war veterans did.

“Isaiah displayed that spirit when God asked ‘Whom shall I send?’ He didn’t give excuses, he didn’t say I am not qualified enough or I have too many responsibilities, or I am too young or I am too old. He simply said, ‘Here I am, send me.’ That is the heart of a willing servant. God expects the same of you and me, He’s asking us that same question today. As our world shows signs of economic shocks and geopolitical uncertainty God is asking who is willing, who will stand for truth, who will serve?” Carlyle told the congregation.

Earlier, in her welcome, RAFA President Major (Retired) Johanna Lewin shared that the founding members of the organisation, formed on August 16, 1946, were a band of merry men who served in the Royal Air Force during World Ward II and did so with a deep sense of pride.

RAFA, she said, initially was for those who served in the war and returned home to Jamaica “to continue their camaraderie and visit the proverbial river — the bar”.

“They wanted to ensure that all was not forgotten and that the comradeship and shared sense of duty that they developed during the war years were persevered. How many of you are familiar with Colonel Reggie Chin, who was commanding officer of the Third Battalion for many years and who served with RAF during the war? How many of you are familiar with Michael Manley, former [Jamaica] prime minister, who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force during World War II? We could be here all day. It’s a long story and cannot be given justice here,” Lewin said.

She shared that RAFA started under a hut at one end of the airfield at the JDF Air Wing in Up Park Camp.

“We were offered three prime camp locations, but the one selected was what we know as Curphey Place in Swallowfield, the home of RAFA and the Jamaica Legion. The land was eventually given in perpetuity for the benefit of veterans. RAFA evolved and became more than just a means for these sassy World War II veterans to visit the ever-present river and chat and reminisce and sing about their experiences in Britain,” Lewin said.

“One of the early and major philanthropic works took place when the British charity… established Cheshire Homes, what we would term a hospice. RAFA was the first local entity to pledge $10,000, a tidy sum in those days, to build one of the units. Cheshire Homes is what we now know as the Mona Rehab. We were able to fund the original columbarium in Briggs Park and now the extension. RAFA has continued its tradition of raising funds and giving,” Lewin said.

World.title: First hurdle cleared
World.content:
KOZYCKI... campaign focused on fighting corruption, working to rebuild trust in Government; tackling affordability, lowering the costs for working families; and expanding access to affordable and quality health care

NEW YORK, USA — The Georgia-based attorney who says he was inspired to run for a seat in the United States Congress to help deportees like Jamaican Godfrey Wade has cleared the first hurdle, winning the Democratic Party’s primary in the state’s 7th Congressional District.

Tony Kozycki, an immigration lawyer, said he was disgusted by the system when he represented Jamaican-born US veteran Godfrey Wade and discovered how difficult it was to get him his day in court for a repaid bounced cheque and an unproven assault charge 12 years ago.

Wade, who lived legally in the US for 50 years, served overseas in the military and was honourably discharged. After being flagged for the offences he was deported to Jamaica earlier this year. Kozycki has since been fighting the case, with little success. He never became a US citizen.

Asked for an update on the case, the attorney told the Jamaica Observer, which carried the deportation story, that there had not been any major new legal developments or petitions filed on Wade’s behalf.

“However, we have not given up, as I still believe Godfrey deserves the opportunity to return to the United States and have his case heard fairly. We continue to advocate for him and remain committed to seeing him receive the process he deserves,” said Kozycki.

“Wade’s case did more than expose a broken immigration system, it exposed a failure of representation by Rich McCormick,” Kozycki added.

McCormick is the Republican attorney, an incumbent whom Kozycki will face in the midterm elections for the Georgia 7th Congressional District, after snagging the Democratic Party nomination by polling 19,742 or 40 per cent of the votes against nearest rival Case Norton’s 11,036 or 22.3 per cent.

The other two contestants polled a combined 36,000 votes in the May 2026 primary. Kozycki returned to defeat filmmaker Norton in the run-off, after garnering 11,667 to Norton’s 5,561 votes.

Kozycki accused McCormick of failing to provide adequate representation for Wade.

Both he and Wade have consistently maintained that notices for the Jamaican to attend a hearing were never received, due to problems with an address used by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which they say courts records show.

Moreover, restitution of the bounced cheque and all applicable fees were made in full, according to Wade’s family. His attorney noted that no physical violence was ever alleged in the assault charge.

“All we are asking is for the case to be reopened and Mr Wade to have his day in court. There is no need to trust me or Godfrey, just look at the documents and the evidence. All we want is one day before a judge and I know we will win this case,” Kozycki told the Observer during an interview in March this year.

As for his campaign priorities, Kozycki said they centre on three issues: “Fighting corruption and working to rebuild trust in Government, tackling affordability and lowering the costs for working families, and expanding access to affordable and quality health care.”

There are significant Jamaican and other Caribbean communities in the metro Atlanta area which forms part of Georgia’s 7th Congressional District, something which has not been lost on Kozykic and his campaign.
