World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.title: ‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.content:
Yan Bowen’s only attempt to get a credit card came during her first year at university. The bank rejected her because she had no income, reinforcing her belief that cards were meant for “people with stable incomes.”

Then, at 22, she found herself in debt anyway.

Last October, she realized she owed around 3,000 yuan ($400) — more than her entire monthly student allowance. With the debt weighing on her, she cut daily expenses, took on part-time work, and borrowed from friends to pay it down.

The debt had built up through apps she used every day to order takeout, buy groceries, and shop online, each offering the option to pay later or split purchases into installments.

Even so, Yan sees the relatively low limits on app-based credit as a safeguard against getting in too deep. “It keeps the risk manageable, nothing big enough to shock my parents,” she said. “A credit card would just mean higher risk.”

That wariness extends well beyond Yan. By the end of March 2026, China had about 687 million credit and combo cards in circulation, down roughly 120 million from their 2022 peak, according to central bank data.

Yan is one of 12 people aged 20 to 26, including students, job seekers, and office workers, whom Sixth Tone interviewed in July. Of them, nine had never owned a credit card. Many knew little about how cards worked and worried most about missing repayments. The few who did use cards tended to do so for specific reasons, such as overseas travel or managing cash flow.

More than 60 credit card subcenters closed across China in 2025, according to state-run People’s Daily, while some banks folded their card businesses and standalone apps into broader retail operations.

Yet outstanding balances on bank cards have remained relatively stable, said Jiang Jiajun, an associate professor at Fudan University’s School of Economics, in Shanghai. That suggests many of the cards being canceled were dormant rather than evidence that consumers had stopped borrowing. Even so, he said, “at least from the data, there is a clear trend of people avoiding credit cards.”

The traditional selling points — higher limits, longer interest-free periods, and richer rewards — may simply matter less to younger consumers. Those perks “are not necessarily what Gen Z cares most about,” Jiang said.

Yan’s first encounter with borrowing came through a food-delivery coupon. During her sophomore year, Chinese delivery app Meituan offered her a discount worth less than 1 yuan, but only if she activated its pay-later service. She did.

Before long, she had signed up for Huabei, a credit service inside Ant Group’s Alipay payment app, and Baitiao, a similar product from e-commerce giant JD.com. “They’re just so easy,” Yan said. “Even when traveling, hotels let you stay first and pay later.”

Even with enough money in the bank, Yan sometimes chose to pay later or in installments rather than watch her balance fall. Small debts piled up across different apps, and she often did not know the total until the monthly bill came due.

Her biggest current debt comes from a 6,500-yuan laptop. To be eligible for a student discount, Yan had to pay through Baitiao, so she split the cost into six monthly installments of more than 1,000 yuan. As of Aug. 5, she still owed more than 5,600 yuan.

Unlike credit cards, which require a separate application, app-based credit is built directly into services young consumers already use, often with lower limits and fewer steps between browsing and borrowing.

Jiang said the difference comes down partly to “mental accounting” — the way people sort spending into different mental buckets. Small, frequent purchases through apps like Huabei can feel like part of a “convenient lifestyle” rather than “financial debt.” Credit cards, by contrast, make the borrowing harder to ignore.

“They make users acutely aware that they are borrowing money, which naturally triggers resistance,” Jiang said. “These two things sit in completely different mental accounts for young people.”

For some young consumers, credit cards begin to look more useful as purchases get bigger and finances more secure.

Wang Xuanren, 23, works in finance in the eastern city of Nanjing and applied for her first and only credit card in 2024 ahead of an overseas trip. She already had more than 500,000 yuan in a fixed-term deposit at the bank, helping her secure approval the same day; the card arrived five days later.

She now saves it largely for electronics and luxury goods. For big-ticket purchases, Wang said installments can turn a 40,000- or 50,000-yuan expense into much smaller monthly payments, automatically deducted from her debit account.

“I keep a lot of cash on hand,” she said. “Using a credit card interest-free is basically borrowing someone else’s money and paying it back later.”

Zheng Yuxin, a 21-year-old university student in Shanghai, is far less comfortable with that bargain. She has no plans to apply for a credit card or use app-based credit anytime soon. “Nothing in life is free,” she said.

Even generous sign-up bonuses make her wary. Credit cards feel “very distant and risky,” she said. “I worry about falling for a scam because I can’t tell what’s real.”

In 2023, Zheng activated Huabei after agreeing to an authorization screen and completing facial verification. It then became her default payment method, allowing later purchases to be charged through the service without her actively choosing it each time.

She realized what had happened only when roughly 100 yuan was deducted from her bank account on repayment day. “Seeing unexpected money disappear gave me this empty, unsettled feeling,” she said. Since then, she has stuck to a simpler rule: buy only when she already has the money.

From Sept. 30, China will require a clearer separation between paying and borrowing online. Non-bank payment providers will no longer be allowed to present loans as payment options or market lending products through their payment services, with companies required to adjust their practices before the rules take effect.

Jiang said such rules should make borrowing more transparent and give users clearer warnings before they take on debt. The goal, he said, is not to eliminate app-based credit, but to make sure consumers know when an ordinary purchase has become a loan. “This protects consumers and helps platforms earn long-term trust,” he said.

Those preferences may change with age. Higher incomes, more travel, and larger spending needs could eventually make the higher limits and longer interest-free periods of credit cards more useful. “The same group of people might develop completely different habits 10 years from now,” said Jiang.

Zhang Xinyun, 24 and from the northeastern city of Harbin, is currently unemployed and remains deeply wary of credit cards after watching a relative struggle with card debt when she was a teenager. “Spending ahead always comes with bad temptations,” she said. High limits look more like added risk than freedom, and sign-up gifts do little to reassure her.

But Zhang can imagine her needs changing. Once she starts working or running a business, she said, a card could become useful for managing cash flow or traveling overseas.

Jiang underscores that banks cannot rely on that change happening on its own. “They need to improve convenience, embrace fintech, and create use cases that resonate with younger consumers.”

At the bank where Zhao Wei works in the northeastern city of Shenyang, signing up new credit card users is part of the job. She is expected to bring in dozens each year and, last year, even opened her own first card partly to help meet the target.

Many customers worry about missing repayments and damaging their credit records, Zhao said. Others simply see little need for a card when mobile payments and app-based credit are already woven into daily spending through digital services such as WeChat Pay, Alipay, and Huabei.

Banks have responded with incentives. Zhao’s gives new cardholders 150 yuan in spending credits, along with gifts ranging from rice and cooking oil to household appliances. Elsewhere, welcome offers can include health checkups, airport lounge access, fuel vouchers, coffee coupons, and cash back on purchases.

Zhao is blunt about how far such incentives can go. “People who are put off by credit cards won’t open one just for that,” she said.

More recently, her bank began offering customized cards printed with customers’ pet photos, along with discounts on pet supplies.

Even that has not made Zhao optimistic. “Credit cards are being squeezed by more convenient products,” she said. “If they can’t build stronger ties to daily life, becoming obsolete is not impossible.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.title: Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.content:
A Chinese county known as the home of over 400 temple murals dating back to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) is facing a heritage restoration crisis, with many of its murals stolen, destroyed, or marred by thieves.

In an investigation published Wednesday, Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper visited 16 fortified villages in Yu County in the northern Hebei province and found that many of the area’s temple murals had been stolen, destroyed during temple collapse, or weathered beyond recognition. Remaining fragments often bore looters’ cut marks.

A major cultural relic hub, the county served as a military and commercial crossroads during the Ming and Qing dynasties (1644–1911) and is home to more than 1,600 registered cultural heritage locations, including numerous fortified villages. The accompanying temples feature murals depicting Taoist, Buddhist, and folk religious elements.

Danhou Village — inscribed on China’s official list of traditional villages in 2016 — is one of the county’s most popular tourist destinations. The village’s Guandi Temple was once home to extensive murals, but only fragments remain today.

When The Paper visited, the temple was under renovation for leaking roofs, missing wooden components, and cracked walls after years of neglect. Work began in April and is projected to be completed by the end of the year.

Of the 16 villages The Paper visited, only those officially considered “traditional villages” or protected sites received restoration and care. The report noted that overall neglect of the fortified villages stems from their abandonment, as villagers have mostly lived outside the sites since the 1980s, leaving the buildings to decay.

A member of the county’s cultural relics management office told The Paper that he recently inspected a temple on a visit to his hometown.

“I went there around noon, and the wall was still standing,” he said. “But at around 2 p.m., I got a call saying the western wall of that temple had collapsed. If I had gone any later, I might have been buried under it.”

Another obstacle to upkeep is funding. Under China’s cultural relics law, their owners or users must preserve them, with government subsidies provided where possible. But in Yu County, most low-level relics are owned by villages that can’t afford maintenance, placing the burden on the county.

The cultural relics worker described how every village has an appointed relic steward, but with no subsidy budget, the role falls to village cadres as an additional duty. With heavy workloads and no stipends, protection relies on individual goodwill.

Yet government investment has been considerable. Over a decade ago, Yu County built a 12,000-square-meter museum for 10,000-plus movable relics, free to the public, costing the county nearly 4 million yuan ($600,000) annually. In 2023, state and provincial funds for restoration projects totaled 14.6 million yuan.

Despite the investment, Yu County’s neglected relics expose gaps in China’s heritage architecture protection, a problem that it has been working to solve in recent years.

In July 2024, the Finance Ministry created a lottery-funded program for unlisted ancient buildings. Upon submitting a proposal, local authorities whose heritage architecture and restoration projects are deemed to serve the public good are given priority. The program will run through 2027.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Murals at an ancient temple in Yu County, Hebei province, June 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.title: The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.content:
During the opening decades of the 15th century, a eunuch from China’s imperial court led seven epic voyages across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, pushing westward as far as the Red Sea and the shores of East Africa.

The expeditions were astonishing feats of engineering and navigation. Setting sail decades before Christopher Columbus or Vasco da Gama, Zheng spent years crossing the oceans at the head of a vast fleet of 200 ships. Some of the vessels measured up to 70 meters long — three times the size of Columbus’ ships.

For many, Zheng deserves to rank among history’s greatest explorers. Yet, much about the voyages — and Zheng himself — remains shrouded in mystery. He barely features in the official records left by China’s Ming dynasty (1368–1644), with court historians dismissing his expeditions as impressive, but ruinously expensive. Even the place and date of Zheng’s death are unknown.

The Ming court’s assessment still colors views of Zheng centuries later. Today, the great admiral is well known in China, with generations of schoolchildren learning about his amazing treasure ships that brought giraffes, lions, zebras, and other exotic beasts back from Africa. But the voyages tend to be presented as a historical curiosity that had little lasting impact.

Zou Zhenhuan is on a mission to change that. The 69-year-old — now a distinguished professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University — has spent decades studying Zheng He, and his research has played a significant role in shifting perceptions of the explorer and his legacy. His latest book, “Monsoon Asia and Africa: Cultural Exchange and Zheng He’s Voyages,” is his most comprehensive look at the subject yet.

For Zou, Zheng’s voyages were far more influential than often assumed. Far from a flash in the pan, they opened up a new era of maritime trade between Asia and Africa, as merchants took advantage of the navigational technologies and sea routes pioneered by Zheng. He even believes they helped pave the way for the European Age of Discovery that followed.

In this interview, Zou, who is also a research fellow at the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History, explains why Zheng He is often so misunderstood — and why his voyages should be seen as a harbinger of globalization. The text has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: You have studied Zheng He for more than 20 years. What drew you to this subject in the beginning?

Zou: My interest in Zheng He began in my boyhood. What captivated me most was his extraordinary perseverance — seven voyages spanning more than two decades. Such marvelous experiences are enough to stir the imagination. As the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões wrote in “Os Lusíadas,” the true and marvelous deeds of brave men surpass all fantasy and legend. I was a sickly boy, but I harbored an intense hero complex, and Zheng He’s exploits answered it perfectly.

It was this interest that led me to study Zheng He once I became a historian, and it is this same interest that has sustained my research for so many years.

Sixth Tone: After all these years of research, what kind of person is Zheng He in your mind?

Zou: As my research has deepened, the image of Zheng He in my mind has grown ever richer. Take his religious faith, for example. Many people might assume Zheng He was simply a Muslim. He was indeed born into a Muslim family; his grandfather and father both made the hajj to Mecca. But he was also a devout Buddhist who was accepted as a disciple by an eminent monk, receiving the Dharma name “Fushan,” and supervising the construction of the Great Bao’en Temple in Nanjing. At the same time, Zheng He was also an adherent of Confucianism. Historical records describe him as “endowed with the talent to govern and versed in the teachings of Confucius and Mencius.”

The most famous material testimony to Zheng He’s plural faith is the trilingual stele he erected in the kingdom of Ceylon (present-day Sri Lanka) during his second voyage in 1409. The stele, commonly known as the Galle Trilingual Inscription, is carved in three scripts: the Chinese text praises the Buddha and records a list of offerings; the Tamil text glorifies the Hindu god Shiva; and the Persian text extols Allah. Paying tribute to the deities of three great religions on a single stone tablet is, in my view, the most vivid expression of Zheng He’s cosmopolitan, all-embracing spirit.

Sixth Tone: It seems “plurality” is a keyword when it comes to Zheng He.

Zou: Exactly. Zheng He was a man of all-around talent. To begin with, he possessed exceptional organizational and managerial abilities — commanding a fleet of more than 27,000 men was in itself an enormously complex feat of systems engineering.

He also had the metaphysical learning of a Confucian scholar and was equally adept at practical, technical matters: during the voyages he spread the Chinese calendar, rituals, weights and measures, and architectural techniques to other countries, and with superb diplomatic skill he mediated disputes between Siam and Malacca, and between Annam and Champa.

Plus, he even displayed outstanding military talent: on his very first voyage he defeated Chen Zuyi, a pirate chief who commanded tens of thousands of followers in the Strait of Malacca, wiping out more than 5,000 pirates.

Sixth Tone: When I was reading your book, what impressed me most was Zheng He’s nautical technology — especially his precise understanding and ingenious use of the Indian Ocean monsoons.

Zou: That’s right. The fleet’s seven expeditions were deeply embedded in the monsoon, which is the main reason I titled the book “Monsoon Asia and Africa.”

The regions the fleet traversed — East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Indian Ocean — are among the areas of the world where the monsoon phenomenon is most pronounced. And in an era without modern propulsion, the monsoon was the “engine” that drove this enormous armada on its long voyages.

The fleet usually departed China in winter, between October and March, riding the northeast monsoon southward. By the time it reached the Indian Ocean, the summer southwest monsoon would be blowing, allowing a smooth voyage home. The whole round trip took about a year and a half.

To visit more places efficiently, Zheng He would dispatch detached squadrons along the way; after completing their missions, these squadrons would regroup at designated rendezvous points in accordance with the monsoon patterns.

But here’s the thing: the monsoon and the compass could carry the fleet forward, but they could not tell the crew exactly where they were on the open sea. To do this, the fleet mastered a refined technique known as “guoyang qianxing,” or star-observation navigation, using an instrument called the “qianxing,” or star-measuring, board to determine a ship’s latitude according to stars’ altitude above the horizon. Zheng He’s fleets also compiled these observations into dedicated star charts, creating a reusable navigational database.

One could say that Zheng He’s fleet fused three techniques — the monsoon patterns, star-observation navigation, and the magnetic compass — into a single, world-leading navigational system for its time. I believe these sea routes, nautical technology, and geographical knowledge helped lay the intellectual and technical foundations for the arrival of European explorers more than half a century later. However, this topic needs further research.

Sixth Tone: Since you mention the European explorers who came later, I have to raise a common critique: that unlike the explorers who launched Europe’s Age of Discovery, Zheng He’s expeditions — for all their grandeur — were a mere flash in the pan that left no lasting imprint. How do you see it?

Zou: This view is indeed very common. I would point out that Zheng He’s seven voyages were not merely official acts of diplomacy by the Ming court; they also facilitated exchanges of goods, species, and technologies between Asia and Africa on an unprecedented scale.

The exotic animals the fleet brought back from foreign lands — giraffes, lions, ostriches, zebras — and the rare plants and fruits such as pepper, sappanwood, and durian greatly enriched China’s native stock of species. Wherever it went, the fleet shared nautical and astronomical knowledge with local peoples, deepening mutual learning among the civilizations of Asia and Africa.

The most representative example of all this is blue-and-white porcelain. Zheng He’s fleet carried large quantities of porcelain into the Islamic world, while the cobalt pigment needed to produce blue-and-white ware, known as “Sumali blue,” originally came from Persia. This pattern of “bringing finished products out and importing raw materials in” was itself a cross-cultural dialogue of technology and aesthetics.

As the Ming dynasty’s most sought-after export in overseas markets, blue-and-white porcelain was among the important gifts carried on every mission. Pieces dating from the period of Zheng He’s voyages have been unearthed at Fustat in Egypt, at Aydhab in Sudan, at Aden on the Arabian Peninsula, and elsewhere.

The huge overseas demand, in turn, stimulated a massive increase in early Ming porcelain production: according to historical records, in 1433 alone the court ordered the firing of 443,500 pieces in a single decree.

What does this tell us? It shows that nearly a century before Columbus set sail, Zheng He’s fleet had already opened up the east-west sea routes of the Indian Ocean and built a regional network of trade and cultural exchange. I call this the “Zheng He exchange.”

Sixth Tone: That concept readily brings to mind the “Columbian exchange” — the massive exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that opened up after Columbus’ voyages.

Zou: I did indeed borrow the theoretical framework of the “Columbian exchange,” but my concept points to an earlier wave of civilizational interaction — one that unfolded between Asia and Africa. In many respects, Zheng He was a key catalyst on the eve of globalization.

Of course, while the “Zheng He exchange” and the “Columbian exchange” share many similarities, their purposes were fundamentally different. Zheng He’s voyages never established colonies overseas, and they were extremely restrained in their use of force.

As you mentioned, many Chinese people feel rather regretful about this, believing it caused China to miss a golden opportunity to dominate the globe. Liu Cixin’s short science-fiction story “Xiyang” (“The Western Ocean”) expresses exactly this sentiment through an alternate-history framework: in the story, Zheng He’s fleet sails farther west from the East African coast, rounds the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually reaches Europe, defeats the combined Anglo-French forces, and conquers the European continent, turning China into an empire on which the sun never sets.

But in my view, Zheng He radiates the light of pacifism and cultural pluralism — and that is precisely where his example can offer inspiration for our own time.

(Header image: A statue of Zheng He in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, 2024. 500px Essential)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.title: An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.content:
“My contact lenses are comfortable even after wearing them all day. Do you want to try them?”

So says a young woman in glasses with transparent lenses, in response to a friend who says her contacts are painful. She then takes a contact box out of a black handbag, offers it, and says, “You can blink without worry.”

The endorsement seems genuine enough — except neither woman is real.

This , featuring the popular AI actress Fang Taozi endorsing colored contacts, has recently sparked controversy in China over whether an AI character can vouch for a product’s quality.

Released in late July on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by domestic contact lens brand Nutnutlook, the ad was taken down without comment last week.

In response, Chinese netizens criticized the  for using an AI avatar instead of a human actress. “What makes me uncomfortable is that someone without eyes now has the right to speak about eyes,” one user commented.

“AI doesn’t even know what it feels like to actually wear the product,” another wrote.

Neither the company behind the AI actress, Guangzhou-based World Media Film and TV Culture, nor the contacts brand has responded to the controversy.

The fictional 20-year-old Fang Taozi was unveiled in the AI short drama “The Laid-off Girl” in June this year. The series, which tells the story of a small-town girl moving to a fictional city to pursue a modeling career, has been viewed more than 320 million times on Douyin.

In the months following the series’ release, directed by popular content creator Fei Feifei, Fang’s personal Douyin account — created by companies to boost AI actors’popularity — gained more than 470,000 followers. Her account posts content ranging from so-called “behind-the-scenes” footage during the show’s production to snippets of her supposed daily life, such as making breakfast.

Fang has been lauded by fans for having, unlike many AI characters, moles and blemishes, giving her an imperfect and realistic appearance. In “The Laid-off Girl,” she struggles with relatable Chinese workplace challenges, such as pressure to attend business dinners and getting bullied by her colleagues.

Domestic media reported that on Juliang Xingtu, Douyin’s influencer marketing platform, Fang Taozi’s advertising rates are 168,000 yuan ($24,900) per video for clips under 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan for videos between 21 and 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan for videos over 60 seconds — significantly higher than ad rates charged by most human influencers.

Ma Lihong, a senior partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, told domestic media that, despite AI avatars not being considered people under Chinese law and therefore not legally considered  endorsers, the video could still constitute false advertising.

Ma added that advertisers are responsible for the truthfulness of their content and that by making a first-person claim about experiencing a product, the AI character could be seen as fabricating user experience. As such, the brand and the ’s producer could potentially be in violation of the law.

Compounding the severity of the issue, colored contact lenses are classified as Class III medical devices under China’s regulatory system, reserved for items that pose the highest risk to consumers. Actors are prohibited from recommending such products in s, a rule aimed at preventing brands from misleading consumers.

This is not the first time Chinese brands have experimented with AI-generated figures in advertising. Major bottled water company Nongfu Spring made headlines last year for using AI-generated images in promotional posters, while companies ranging from yogurt brands to office chair suppliers have collaborated with various AI-generated actors to endorse products and use slogans. Tutorials on using AI-generated videos for livestream commerce have also become common.

Entertainment law expert Qiu Zhimiao said AI-powered endorsements will become increasingly common, and regulating them is a new frontier. As s endorsed by virtual influencers exist in a legal gray area, he said, there is a need for clearer regulations.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of the AI actress Fang Taozi in the  promoting colored contact lenses. From Weibo)

World.title: Iran threatens to go on offensive in Strait of Hormuz if diplomacy with US fails
World.content:
A vessel near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 17, 2026. REUTERS/

Today marks the day by which Iran and the United States are expected to reach a final deal under a memorandum of understanding agreed in June and aimed at ending the war

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Iran has decided to shift its policy from defensive to “fully offensive” due to the deadlock in efforts to agree a permanent end to its war with the United States, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday, August 17.

Progress towards peace talks and a resumption of oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz has ground to a halt, with no sign that the warring parties are moving towards ending the conflict that the US and Israel launched on February 28.

“Iranian entities must be prepared to escalate tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and wider region, as Iran will be ready to make decisions and take action on difficult decisions,” the Iranian official said, adding that Tehran would conduct a “timely and precise” military attack to break the US naval blockade if diplomacy failed.

Monday marked the day by which Iran and the United States were expected to reach a final deal under a memorandum of understanding agreed in June and aimed at ending the war.

Signed on June 17, the MoU set out a 60-day timeframe, extendable by mutual consent, by which Washington and Tehran should reach an agreement that would cover broader issues such as the fate of Iran’s nuclear program.

The MoU, which declared the immediate and permanent cessation of military operations on all fronts, quickly unraveled, however, due to a dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran to set deadline

Tehran said point 5 of the MoU gives it the right to manage the waterway, while Washington rejected that interpretation. Hostilities resumed as Tehran began firing on vessels it said were trying to sail through the waterway on an unapproved route.

US President Donald Trump said on July 7 that the pact was “over.” Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of consistently violating its commitments.

“Within the short period of a few weeks set by Iran, all the agreement’s provisions must be implemented by the US. This is a precondition for further negotiations with the US,” the Iranian official told Reuters, adding that mediators would share Tehran’s deadline with Washington and regional states.

Both Iran and the United States have stepped up rhetoric over the past week.

Trump warned Americans in a speech at a rally on Friday, August 14, to prepare for continued high fuel prices as a result of the war, while also saying that “after we finish defeating Iran … pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform: “The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon,” repeating one of his stated rationales for the war. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial postponed again due to bad weather
World.content:
IMPEACHMENT. The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte begins at the Senate on July 6, 2026.

This is the second time the impeachment court has postponed a trial session due to bad weather. The first was last August 10.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court on Monday, August 17, postponed the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte scheduled for Tuesday, August 18, citing the forecast of heavy rain and flooding due to the southwest monsoon or habagat.

Senate President Win Gatchalian also allowed all Senate officials and employees to work from home on Tuesday.

This is the second time the impeachment court has postponed a trial session due to bad weather. The first was on Monday, August 10.

Malacañang also suspended face-to-face classes in public and private schools and ordered government offices in Metro Manila and several other provinces to shift to work-from-home arrangements on Monday.

The House prosecution was supposed to continue its direct examination of its witness, Gina Acosta, former special disbursing officer of the Office of the Vice President under Duterte. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Bulk’ of Gilas Pilipinas crew for Asian Games to feature new players
World.content:
SQUAD. June Mar Fajardo (15), Scottie Thompson (9), and Dwight Ramos (24) in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the FIBA World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers.

Head coach Tim Cone says Gilas Pilipinas will 'pretty much bring an all-PBA contingent' to the Asian Games, where the Philippines will try to defend its crown

MANILA, Philippines – A rejigged roster vastly different from the Gilas Pilipinas’ lineup in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers will try to defend the Philippines’ throne in the Asian Games.

Head coach Tim Cone said the “bulk” of the Philippines’ Asian Games squad will be new faces as the team grapples with the unavailability of Filipino imports who play in the Japan B. League and Korean Basketball League.

B. League standouts Dwight Ramos, AJ Edu, Quentin Millora-Brown, and Mike Phillips, as well as KBL stalwarts Kevin Quiambao and Carl Tamayo, are expected to miss the quadrennial showpiece, leaving half the squad unfilled.

Much like the 2023 edition, where the Gilas Pilipinas ended a six-decade gold-medal drought, the country will once again be represented mostly by PBA players led by Barangay Ginebra resident import Justin Brownlee.

“None of the Japan or Korea players can play in the Asian Games. So, we just decided that we would pretty much bring an all-PBA contingent for the Asian Games, along with Justin,” said Cone.

PBA players not part of the current national team but included in the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas’ 30-man pool for the Asian Games are TNT’s Jordan Heading and Brandon Ganuelas-Rosser, Rain or Shine’s Adrian Nocum and Caelan Tiongson, Converge’s Justin Arana, NLEX’s Robert Bolick, Blackwater’s Sedrick Barefield, Magnolia’s Zavier Lucero, San Miguel’s Don Trollano and Jerrick Ahanmisi, Phoenix’s Jason Perkins, and Meralco’s Brandon Bates.

Of course, national team holdovers June Mar Fajardo and CJ Perez of San Miguel, Scottie Thompson, RJ Abarrientos, and Troy Rosario of Barangay Ginebra, Calvin Oftana of TNT, Juan Gomez de Liaño and Justine Baltazar of Converge, and Chris Newsome of Meralco were included.

Fajardo, however, is uncertain for the Asian Games as Cone bared that the nine-time PBA MVP had wanted to retire from national team duties but agreed to play in the fourth window of the Asian Qualifiers this August due to the Philippines’ manpower issues, with big men Millora-Brown, Phillips, and Kai Sotto set to sit out.

Sotto is another major question mark for the Asian Games, with Cone saying there is “no word” on whether the 7-foot-3 star will suit up.

“One or two or three from the window team to join. But the bulk of the team will be new,” said Cone.

Cone also has his fingers crossed that Benny Boatwright will make it in time for the Asian Games, as the bill granting him Filipino citizenship still needs the signature of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“We’re hoping that Benny would be all right to play in the Asian Games — that looks very doubtful at this point. But we’re still holding out hope,” said Cone.

The basketball competitions of the Asian Games to be staged in Nagoya, Japan, will tip off on September 10, earlier than the official start of the continental showdown on September 19.

Gilas Pilipinas got bunched with powerhouse China, Bahrain, and Kazakhstan in Group C.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Pax Silica not in proposed 2027 budget as economic managers say nothing final yet
World.content:
If it pushes through, Pax Silica's lease income is expected to 'far outweigh' the costs of managing the proposed New Clark City hub, according to Finance Secretary Frederick Go

MANILA, Philippines – The Marcos administration has not allocated money for the planned Pax Silica industrial hub in the proposed 2027 national budget, with economic managers stressing that the project remains in preliminary discussions and no final agreement has been signed.

Finance Secretary Frederick Go made the clarification during House deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget after Gabriela Representative Sarah Elago asked whether government agencies had set aside funding for the United States-led initiative.

“There’s nothing in the budget that will spend for this proposed industrial hub because nothing has been signed,” Go said on Monday, August 17. “It’s still a discussion.”

Play Video

Acting Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon also confirmed that there is no allocation in the National Expenditure Program intended for Pax Silica. He clarified that the increase Elago cited under the Department of Information and Communications Technology is for implementation of the government’s e-government mandate, not the proposed hub.

Pax Silica is a US-led initiative aimed at strengthening supply chains for technologies ranging from critical minerals and semiconductors to advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence.

The Philippines joined the initiative in April, with plans being discussed for a roughly 4,000-acre industrial and innovation hub in New Clark City in Tarlac, though no detailed agreements governing the proposed project have been signed.

Go said that if the New Clark City development eventually proceeds, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) should earn more from the project than it spends managing the property.

“They will pay us rent. So it is a revenue-enhancing project,” Go said. He later added that “the revenue should far outweigh any project management expense like in any other real estate venture.”

The BCDA earlier said it would grant a two-year grace period on lease payments as an in-kind Philippine contribution to the initiative, with rental rates from the third year onward to be determined under a subsequent agreement. The final commercial terms have yet to be negotiated.

Why government wants Pax Silica

The attraction for the Philippines is the possibility of moving beyond its traditional reliance on consumption and services toward higher-value manufacturing.

At the Economic Journalists Association of the Philippines forum, Economy Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said the country needs to diversify its sources of growth by generating more investment and exports, while rebuilding industry and revitalizing agriculture. He noted that the Philippine economy had behaved like a richer economy dominated by services even before developing a sufficiently deep industrial base.

Balisacan said the country still has an opportunity to industrialize, particularly by attracting industries that raise productivity and create better-paying jobs. He also highlighted the importance of worker upskilling as AI and other emerging technologies reshape the economy.

During the budget hearing, Balisacan said Pax Silica could fit that strategy if it succeeds in attracting advanced technology industries such as semiconductors and electronics.

“That is very consistent with what I was saying earlier that we need to attract industries that bring the quality of jobs higher,” he said.

The BCDA has projected that the New Clark City development could eventually attract $40 billion to $70 billion in investment and generate more than 130,000 high-quality jobs, although these remain government projections for a project that has yet to be finalized.

The potential gains also come with large requirements. Government officials have acknowledged concerns surrounding power and water demand, environmental impact, and indigenous peoples’ rights, while the Department of Energy has said the project must not leave the rest of the country at a disadvantage as it secures the substantial electricity supply required by an advanced manufacturing hub. (READ: Why Energy Secretary Garin says Pax Silica is ‘too dangerous’ to plug into grid) – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No plans to merge Araling Panlipunan and MAPEH – DepEd
World.content:
In a statement on August 8, the Department of Education clarified that the post circulating online is based on an outdated report

Claim: The Department of Education (DepEd) plans to merge the subjects Araling Panlipunan (Social Studies) and Music, Arts, PE, and Health (MAPEH).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A graphic bearing the claim was posted on August 7 by Carl Balita, an educator and media personality with 3.1 million Facebook followers.

The post featured the official DepEd logo alongside text reading, “DepEd, planong pag-isahin na lang ang Araling Panlipunan at MAPEH (DepEd plans to merge Araling Panlipunan and MAPEH).”

The same graphic was also shared on August 8 by the Facebook page “Hugot pa Teacher,” which has 568,000 followers.

The facts: The posts are based on an outdated report. On August 8, DepEd clarified that the posts were based on an April 2023 PTV News report regarding a proposed merger of the two subjects into one — Sibika, Sining at Kultura, Kasaysayan, at Kagalingang Pangkatawan (SIKAP) — for students from Kindergarten to Grade 3.

While that plan did exist in 2023, DepEd stated that the news item “reflects outdated discussions from 2023 and does not represent current policy.” According to the education department, “Makabansa” serves as a distinct learning area for Grades 1 to 3 under the revised K to 10 curriculum, while Araling Panlipunan and MAPEH will continue to be taught as separate subjects starting in Grade 4.

“We urge the public to practice critical thinking, check context, and verify release dates before sharing content online,” the statement added.

AP and MAPEH: According to a 2013 DepEd curriculum guide, Araling Panlipunan or Social Studies aims to shape critical, reflective, responsible, productive, and patriotic citizens, as well as equip them with an appreciation for historical and social issues.

The subject MAPEH, meanwhile, covers lessons in music, arts, physical education, and health to “culturally enrich students and help them enjoy and learn new things.”

In 2023, DepEd launched its “Matatag” revised K-10 curriculum, which reduces the number of learning areas for students to focus on foundational skills.

Edited caption: Around five hours after DepEd debunked the misleading post on August 8, the “Hugot pa Teacher” page edited its caption.

As of writing, the post now includes a disclaimer stating that the report was based on a 2023 draft proposal. However, the original publication material remains up and continues to circulate online.

Meanwhile, Balita’s post also remains up without any DepEd clarification.

Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked false claims related to DepEd and its curriculum and programs.

– Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is a senior student journalist and an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: From Illicit Wealth to Public Services: Where Kazakhstan’s Recovered Assets Are Going
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has returned 1.154 trillion tenge (US$2.5 billion) in assets to state ownership since launching its asset-recovery program in September 2023. The central question now is how effectively these funds can be converted into long-term public benefits, particularly in regions facing infrastructure shortages.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has repeatedly stressed that the asset-recovery process should serve a broader public purpose.

“The restoration of social justice through the return of illegally acquired assets is not a matter of political expediency or a PR campaign, but a principled position of the state,” Tokayev said in a Jan. 5 interview with the Turkistan newspaper.

The funds are channeled through the Special State Fund, created to finance social and infrastructure projects. According to the General Prosecutor’s Office, 617.6 billion tenge (US$1.3 billion) has been allocated to 466 projects, with water supply, healthcare and education accounting for the largest share. The scale and geographic distribution of this spending indicate that asset recovery is becoming not only a legal and fiscal process, but also a mechanism for addressing regional infrastructure gaps.

From recovered assets to public infrastructure

Of the 1.154 trillion tenge returned, 1.044 trillion tenge (US$2.3 billion) is in cash, while the remainder consists of real estate, company shares, land and other assets. Annual returns increased sharply from 302.5 billion tenge (US$653.9 million) in 2024 to 773.7 billion tenge (US$1.67 billion) in 2025. The fund returned a further 77.7 billion tenge (US$167.9 million) this year.

The Special State Fund has allocated financing for 235 water-supply projects, 190 healthcare facilities, 17 education projects, 11 infrastructure projects, seven transport facilities and six sports facilities, reported Kazinform on Aug. 17.

Implementation has already moved beyond the allocation stage. More than 253 billion tenge (US$546.9 million) has been spent on 364 projects, of which 349 have been commissioned. Completed projects include 188 water-supply facilities, 163 healthcare facilities, seven education facilities, three sports facilities, one transport facility and two infrastructure projects.

The figures show that the program is producing physical assets, but they also highlight an important implementation issue: the impact of returned funds will depend on whether projects address persistent local infrastructure deficits and remain operational over the long term.

Where the money is going

Eastern Kazakhstan received the largest allocation at 78.9 billion tenge (US$170.5 million), followed by North Kazakhstan with 69.4 billion tenge (US$150 million) and Astana with 64.7 billion tenge (US$139.8 million). The lowest allocations went to Shymkent, the Atyrau Region and the Mangystau Region.

These differences do not necessarily reflect a region’s size or economic importance. According to the General Prosecutor’s Office, allocations depend on the number of applications submitted by local authorities, the availability of completed design and cost documentation, project priorities and the severity of infrastructure shortages.

This makes project preparation an important factor in determining access to financing. Regions with clearly prepared projects and pressing infrastructure needs are better positioned to receive funding.

The National Budget Commission decides how funds are distributed. Once financing is approved, projects are implemented under Kazakhstan’s budget legislation and subject to financial control, state audit and treasury procedures.

What to watch next

The program’s success will depend not only on the amount recovered, but on how well the money is used. Key measures will be completed projects, better infrastructure and improved access to essential services.

The long-term goal is to ensure that recovered funds reach regions with the greatest needs and improve people’s quality of life.

World.title: Kazakhstan Deepens University Ties with Japan and South Korea
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding academic and scientific cooperation with leading universities and research institutions in Japan and South Korea. The country seeks to strengthen higher education, research and artificial intelligence (AI) development.

During visits to Seoul and Tokyo in August, Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek met with university leaders and government officials to discuss academic partnerships, joint research, faculty and student exchanges, and workforce development.

Strengthening ties with Japan

In Tokyo, Nurbek held talks with the leadership of Tokyo Metropolitan University and the United Nations University (UNU).

During a meeting with Tokyo Metropolitan University President Takaya Ohashi, the two sides discussed expanding university partnerships, increasing academic mobility and launching joint educational and research projects. Nurbek also invited Ohashi to attend the Strategic Partners Forum, scheduled for November in Astana.

Cooperation with the UNU was another focus of the visit. During talks with the university’s Rector and U.N. Under-Secretary-General Tshilidzi Marwala, the officials discussed expanding collaboration in science, higher education, research and sustainable development.

The two sides also explored ways to expand the university’s presence in Kazakhstan, in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to strengthen international academic partnerships. Marwala accepted an invitation to attend the Strategic Partners Forum in Astana.

The visit builds on growing educational cooperation between Kazakhstan and Japan following Tokayev’s official visit to Tokyo for the inaugural Central Asia-Japan Summit in December 2025. During the summit, Tokayev described human capital as “the main engine of development” and invited Japanese universities to establish branches and educational centers in Kazakhstan.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Japan’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan Yasumasa Iijima said that educational cooperation has become an increasingly important pillar of bilateral relations alongside trade and investment.

Kazakhstan’s efforts to expand international academic partnerships come as the country strengthens its position as Central Asia’s leading higher education hub. In July, Almaty reached its highest-ever position in the QS Best Student Cities 2027 ranking, while the country recorded another year of growth in international student enrollment.

AI partnership with South Korea

In Seoul, Nurbek met South Korea’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon.

The discussions focused on expanding cooperation in science, higher education and AI, including technology transfer, joint research and the training of highly qualified specialists.

One of the key topics was the planned opening of a branch campus of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) in Kazakhstan.

Nurbek also met with KAIST Vice President Jaemin Jung to discuss academic exchanges, joint research projects and cooperation in AI and digital technologies.

Separate meetings with the leadership of Seoul National University and Korea University focused on expanding collaboration in medicine, engineering, information technology and other priority fields. Both universities maintain partnerships with Kazakh higher education institutions.

Educational cooperation between Kazakhstan and South Korea is also expanding through dual-degree programs.

Seoul Cyber University currently partners with Q University, Almaty Humanitarian and Economic University, and Maqsut Narikbayev University (MNU). The expanding partnerships reflect Kazakhstan’s ambition to become a regional hub for AI and digital innovation.

The visits come as Kazakhstan and South Korea deepen broader strategic ties. Earlier this month, Tokayev accepted an invitation to visit Seoul during talks with South Korean Presidential Chief of Staff Kang Hoon-sik.

South Korea has also become an increasingly popular study destination for Kazakh students. According to the Korean Educational Development Institute, 1,516 Kazakh students were enrolled at South Korean universities as of April 1, 2024.

The trend reflects broader educational cooperation between the two countries. Earlier this year, Woosong University opened a branch campus in Turkistan, while exchange partnerships continue to expand across multiple institutions.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Parliamentary Campaign Enters Final Week With Focus on Rule of Law
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election campaign entered its final stretch, with nationally televised debates dominating the campaign. The debates offered voters an opportunity to compare the platforms of the seven competing political parties.

The campaign featured the first-ever team debates involving representatives of all seven parties, broadcast on the Jibek Joly television channel. The week also included a series of one-on-one debates between individual parties.

The debates marked the only occasion during the campaign when parties appeared as full teams rather than individual candidates. The format tested each party’s ability to present a unified position while responding to questions from opponents and viewers. The public could also vote in real time through QR-code polling.

Political observers said the debates signaled the gradual emergence of a more interactive political culture in Kazakhstan, where candidates are expected not only to present policy proposals but also to defend them under public scrutiny.

That growing emphasis on policy differences was also reflected at an Aug. 14 meeting of the Sarap Expert Club in Astana. Experts said voters are increasingly looking beyond broad campaign promises and focusing instead on how parties propose to address issues such as healthcare, education and social protection, including how their policies would be financed and measured.

Rule of law takes center stage

The main theme of the team debate was law and order, focusing on public safety, judicial reform, equality before the law and public trust in state institutions.

The discussion drew public attention as voters looked beyond campaign slogans for concrete proposals to strengthen the country’s legal system.

“The third round of the election debates was particularly intense. Law and order is a topic that concerns everyone. Kazakhstan has accumulated extensive experience in legal reform, and that process continues to evolve. Much has been achieved, but there is always room for improvement,” Kazakh political scientist and historian Daniyar Ashimbayev wrote on his Telegram channel.

The debate also tested the parties’ ability to move beyond technical proposals and discuss broader values shaping the country’s political and legal system.

The televised debate consisted of four rounds.

Representatives explained why voters should support their parties before evaluating their rivals’ election platforms. They then answered live questions from viewers and concluded by making one specific campaign pledge they committed to fulfilling if elected.

The exchanges were often confrontational, with parties challenging each other’s proposals while defending their own policy priorities.

Among political commentators, Ashimbayev singled out the performance of the Adilet Party, represented by prosecutor Aizhan Aimaganova and lawyer Madi Myrzagarayev, chairman of the National Bar Association.

During the debate, Aimaganova stressed that the rule of law rests on three principles: an independent judiciary and law enforcement system, an open and accountable government, and effective protection of citizens.

“The law must apply equally to everyone,” she said, adding that the state should act proactively rather than simply respond to violations.

Ashimbayev described the pair as a “surprisingly effective tandem of experienced legal practitioners.”

Among the party’s proposals, Ashimbayev highlighted measures to reduce crime through better urban infrastructure, expanded digital services for law enforcement agencies and stronger institutions to protect citizens’ rights. He also pointed to the proposal to establish a unified forecasting and analytical center to identify emerging public security risks before they escalate.

Competing for voters

During the debates, Aq Jol Democratic Party and Respublica continued to compete for entrepreneurs and economically liberal voters, with both parties emphasizing business development and market-oriented reforms.

The Auyl Party remained focused on agricultural development and rural communities, reinforcing its traditional electoral base.

Meanwhile, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) and the People’s Party of Kazakhstan concentrated on social policy. While the Baytaq Green Party distinguished itself by emphasizing environmental protection and sustainable development.

The debate attracted a record level of public participation.

According to Jibek Joly, 165,153 viewers cast votes through the broadcast’s QR-code polling system.

The Adilet party received the highest level of public support with 60.6% of the vote, followed by Auyl with 15.1% and Respublica with 10.2%. NSDP received 3.9%, Aq Jol 3.5%, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan 3.3%, and Baytaq 2.7%. Another 0.7% of respondents selected the option “no one.”

The week also featured head-to-head debates between Aq Jol and Respublica, as well as between the NSDP and the People’s Party of Kazakhstan.

According to political analysts and reactions on social media, Aq Jol’s representative adopted a more confrontational style, relying heavily on factual arguments, while Respublica emphasized political renewal and generational change.

The debate between NSDP and the People’s Party focused primarily on ideological differences, social policy and competing approaches to economic development.

As of Aug. 17, three nationally televised debates had taken place, with a fourth and final debate scheduled for Aug. 19 on 24KZ TV channel.

Elections to Kurultai are scheduled for Aug. 23.

On Aug. 12, the Central Election Commission accredited an additional 405 observers, bringing the total number of accredited election observers to 656.

World.title: Caspian Seal Conservation Faces New Challenges as Sea Changes
World.content:
ASTANA – The Caspian Sea is home to the Caspian seal, the world’s only seal species found exclusively in the Caspian Sea. The species spends most of its life in the water and travels considerable distances in search of food, while the northern Caspian’s winter ice fields provide critical breeding grounds.

The main conservation challenge is no longer simply protecting known seal habitats, but adapting protection to a changing Caspian Sea. Declining water levels and warmer winters are affecting traditional breeding and haul-out areas, while pollution, fishing nets and other human activities add to the pressure.

In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal is listed in the Red Book and is protected by law. Scientists are increasingly focused on how environmental changes affect the species and where new protection measures may be needed, according to the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.

A habitat in transition

A documentary by the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, “On the Shoals of the Caspian Sea, the Call of the Seals”, highlights the work of Kazakh researchers. Scientists conduct aerial surveys, locate seal rookeries and analyze population and habitat data.

Assel Baimukanova, a researcher at the institute, said the retreating sea is changing the distribution of suitable habitats.

“As the sea regresses, seals lose their traditional habitats. However, new islands are forming, and it is crucial that they remain safe for the seals,” she said.

This means conservation can no longer focus only on historically known sites. Newly formed islands and shoals may become important resting and breeding areas and require timely protection.

Climate and human pressure

Climate change is adding to existing human-related risks. Caspian seals breed on ice in the northern Caspian during winter, but warmer winters can reduce the availability of suitable ice. Pollution, fishing, shipping, oil activities, tourism and poaching pose additional threats.

“Seals breed on the ice of the northern Caspian, but with warmer winters becoming more frequent, we are facing a critical question: can the species adapt to these changes and survive?” Baimukanova said.

Fishing gear remains a particular concern. Researchers and partner organizations have removed several tonnes of discarded fishing nets and plastic waste from seal habitats during previous conservation campaigns, reducing direct risks to the animals.

From monitoring to regional action

The Caspian seal is also an important indicator of the wider health of the Caspian ecosystem. The sea is home to more than 300 endemic invertebrates, 76 fish species and globally significant populations of migratory birds. As a top predator that moves across the basin, the seal can reflect changes throughout the food chain.

Researchers monitor seal mortality, population structure, habitat and food sources. Satellite imagery identifies new islands and sandbanks that may serve as haul-out sites, while field teams collect water, soil and biological samples.

The problem extends beyond Kazakhstan’s borders. All five Caspian states have ratified regional agreements on marine environmental protection and aquatic biological resources. Kazakhstan established the Caspian Seal State Nature Reserve in 2024, according to Baimukanova, but researchers argue that coordinated transboundary protection will also be needed as habitats shift.

Dr Simon Goodman of the University of Leeds said some decline in the Caspian Sea level is likely to continue even with efforts to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions. Conservation planning should therefore begin early enough to balance biodiversity protection with human interests and wellbeing, he said.

For Kazakhstan, the next challenge is to turn scientific evidence into coordinated conservation measures. Their effectiveness will depend on protecting existing seal habitats, identifying and securing new areas as the Caspian ecosystem evolves, and reducing human pressures from fishing, shipping, pollution and other activities.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Exploration Drive Supports Shift Toward Higher-Value Mining
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding geological and geophysical exploration to strengthen its mineral-resource base and support a strategic shift toward deeper processing and higher-value production.

By the end of this year, exploration is expected to cover 2.2 million square kilometers, with work completed at 25 sites. A key priority is the transition from regional 1:200,000-scale surveys to more detailed 1:50,000 geological mapping (GS-50).

This year, 20 GS-50 projects were launched to identify prospective areas for gold, copper, polymetals, rare earth elements, lithium, tungsten, molybdenum and other strategic minerals, reported the Ministry of Industry and Construction on Aug. 17.

The government has allocated 40.7 billion tenge (US$88 million) for geological surveys and seismic exploration in 2026-2028. Of this, 32.7 billion tenge (US$70.7 million) is allocated to GS-50 projects and 8 billion tenge (US$17.3 million) to seismic exploration. The program also plans six 2D seismic projects in the North Torgai and Shu-Sarysu sedimentary basins.

The program combines airborne geophysics, geochemical and laboratory studies, remote-sensing analysis, drilling and geophysical well logging. Its strategic value is to reduce geological uncertainty and improve the investment case for future mining projects.

From exploration to processing

The exploration program supports Kazakhstan’s strategic objective of moving beyond a predominantly raw-material economy.

At the Astana Mining & Metallurgy Congress 2026 on June 11, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said the country aims to develop deeper processing and competitive value-added production. Over the past two years, more than US$1 billion worth of higher-value mining and metallurgical facilities have been launched.

The approach places greater importance on geological data. David Fogel, assistant secretary of Commerce and Director General of the U.S. and Foreign Commercial Service, said at the congress that mapping and surveying are fundamental to reducing uncertainty and attracting investment.

“If you don’t map the resources and the geography properly, then you’re not going to be very efficient and you’re not going to be able to attract large-scale investment,” Fogel said, adding that artificial intelligence is already transforming geological analysis and surveying.

His remarks underline a key point for Kazakhstan: exploration is not only about identifying deposits, but also about producing the reliable data needed to mobilize large-scale capital.

Tungsten as a test case

The Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty tungsten project illustrates this strategy.

The venture between U.S.-based Cove Capital and Kazakhstan’s Tau-Ken Samruk envisages a full production cycle covering mining, beneficiation and metallurgical processing in Kazakhstan. Cove Capital expects total investment requirements of at least US$1.1 billion, subject to completion of the definitive feasibility study and a final investment decision.

The planned output includes ammonium paratungstate (APT), a higher-value intermediate used to produce tungsten powders, tungsten carbide and other specialized materials.

Existing studies indicate potential combined production of around 12,000 tons of tungsten annually, although final capacity and project economics remain under assessment.

The project demonstrates the distinction between geological potential and commercial production. Kazakhstan’s ability to move projects from exploration and feasibility to financing and operations will determine whether its strategy generates sustained economic value.

International relevance

At AMM 2026, U.S. officials highlighted geological mapping as a way to reduce investment risks, while Saudi Arabia stressed the importance of integrated chains covering mining, processing, logistics and technology.

For Kazakhstan, exploration is therefore becoming the first stage of a wider industrial strategy.

The key indicators ahead will be commercially significant discoveries, progress toward feasibility studies and financing, and the development of processing capacity and supporting infrastructure.

The strategy’s success will ultimately depend not on the amount of territory surveyed, but on how effectively new discoveries are converted into mines, processing facilities and competitive products for global markets.

World.title: China’s Bid for an AI World Order: What’s Behind WAICO
World.content:
Trump locks Europe out of AI models; China presents the counter-proposal — a global AI platform, and everyone’s invited. What Beijing wants and why Europe remains skeptical.

By founding the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), China has created its own international framework for governing artificial intelligence — without the players that have traditionally shaped technology policy. For now.

The founding treaty was signed on July 16, in Shanghai by representatives from 29 countries, with UN Secretary-General António Guterres in attendance. The organization is headquartered in Shanghai. Founding members include Russia, Brazil, Indonesia, Pakistan, Malaysia, Kazakhstan, Kenya, South Africa, Serbia, Belarus, Cuba, Venezuela, and Zambia, among others. The United States, E.U. member states, and India are not participating.

In Chinese diplomatic circles, WAICO is described as a “major step” through which the People’s Republic is answering the Global South’s call for greater participation in AI development. The organization is meant to serve two purposes: spreading AI applications across the Global South and organizing training and seminar programs. The goal, Beijing says, is to use AI “for good.”

Four principles — and a jab at Washington

The conceptual framework rests on four principles that China’s leadership laid out at the first World AI Conference in Shanghai: openness and win-win cooperation, risk awareness, inclusivity, and solidarity in global governance.

Under win-win, Beijing groups scenario-based applications such as AI plus industry and AI plus health — in other words, integrating AI with existing economic sectors. AI must remain safe, reliable, and controllable, the argument goes. China says it is working on technical oversight, early-warning and emergency-response mechanisms, as well as laws, standards, and ethical guidelines. Misuse is to be prevented and AI kept under human control.

China rejects what it calls the overextension of national security — the principle of placing one country’s security above the interests of others. The target is clearly export controls and access restrictions.

Asked whether this language should be read as a response to the short-notice blocking of leading American models for European users, Beijing pointed out that Chinese models are open-source, rendering any accusation of bloc-building moot.

The fourth principle aims at multilateralism. Governance rules and technical standards should be coordinated internationally, and Global South countries should receive support in building their own capacities — to avoid, in China’s phrasing, new historical injustices.

What China is concretely offering

Over the next five years, China intends to provide 5,000 AI training slots for participants from Global South countries. Whether these are degree programs, scholarships, or short-term courses remains unclear. Plans also include AI cooperation centers with organizations such as ASEAN, the African Union, the Arab League, BRICS, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. A flagship project is an AI-powered early-warning system that, according to Chinese sources, forecasts typhoons and other extreme weather events in more than 30 countries.

How China translates technological cooperation into concrete projects — across blocs and without exclusive commitments — is currently on display in Kazakhstan. In June, the Central Asian country agreed with the American firm Firebird on investments of up to ten billion dollars in a computing cluster with up to 100,000 Nvidia GPUs in the coal-mining city of Ekibastuz. A month later, on the sidelines of the AI summit in Shanghai, more than 70 contracts with Chinese partners worth a combined total of over $15 billion were signed. The cross-sector package includes, among other things, a partnership with Huawei, the acquisition of Huawei technology, and further expansion of the data-center site in cooperation with the Hengtong Group.

Open to all — including Europe?

From Beijing’s perspective, an upgrade to an official UN body is not ruled out; the organization is still in its early stages, they say. Nor is EU membership excluded. The organization is in principle open to all and is not aimed exclusively at the Global South.

Beijing dismisses the accusation that the aim is to carve out new spheres of influence. It is not building blocs, the argument goes; the basis of cooperation is consultation and mutual benefit.

Still, the connection to the Digital Silk Road is hard to miss. When it comes to overlaps with the digital component of the Belt and Road Initiative — in areas like digital services, health, and education — the answers remain vague. WAICO programs are described more as a complement to existing relationships.

The European Reading

Sources in Brussels security circles say WAICO is read less as a development initiative than as a strategic instrument. What matters is not the announced training slots or cooperation centers but the question of who will shape infrastructure, technical standards, and digital ecosystems in the years ahead. Countries that adopt Chinese models, networks, and processes early on could find themselves increasingly tied to providers and decision-making centers in Beijing or Shanghai over the long term.

Kazakhstan, however, shows that such cooperation does not necessarily lead to exclusive dependency. Astana is working simultaneously with American and Chinese partners, deploying Nvidia processors while also integrating Huawei and other Chinese providers into the expansion of its digital infrastructure. The government is deliberately keeping multiple technological pathways open rather than fully aligning with either of the two major blocs.

That is precisely what makes the example strategically significant: for many Global South countries, the issue is less about making a geopolitical statement than about accessing capital, computing power, and rapid implementation. The contract goes to whoever most convincingly bundles financing, technology, and infrastructure. For Europe, this is nonetheless a warning: future dependencies will not be determined solely by where systems originate, but above all by who delivers them first and operates them over the long haul.

The EU has been working since 2025 on implementing its concept for AI gigafactories — facilities each housing more than 100,000 advanced AI processors. For now, however, the focus in government offices is mainly on sites, financing, and procurement.

What stands out is the speed at which contracts are being signed and capacities built up elsewhere. Kazakhstan is simultaneously engaging American and Chinese technology companies, while Europe is still translating its own sovereign model into practice. The question is whether the planned pace will be fast enough to keep up with international developments.

In Brussels, digital sovereignty is thus moving to center stage. Europe wants to build its own computing capacity while avoiding long-term dependence on individual foreign providers for critical infrastructure.

Arindrajit Basu of the Carnegie Endowment describes WAICO as a state-centric model that primarily serves Chinese interests. Other Western analyses characterize WAICO as a counterpart to the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative. Participants or countries that have expressed interest in the American format include EU member states, Japan, Australia, and India.

Beijing courts Washington

Notably, Beijing is said to be open to cooperation with the United States. The two countries should extend their hands to each other, diplomatic circles say. AI is a global field, and its development must ultimately work for everyone.

When confronted with the objection that the U.S. administration does not currently appear inclined to cooperate, the response is puzzlement at Washington’s course — along with a reference to jointly supported UN resolutions. In Chinese publications, the line is stated more plainly: it is in the greatest shared interest of both nations that AI serve all of humanity. Following government consultations, a bilateral AI dialogue has also been agreed upon.

Beijing’s multilateral foundation is a UN General Assembly resolution on international AI capacity-building, adopted unanimously on July 1, 2024, which China had introduced. It calls for human-centered, inclusive, and sustainable AI development and special support for developing countries.

Building on that, China points to its own programs: the Global AI Governance Initiative of 2023, a 13-point action plan for global AI governance from 2025, and an AI Capacity-Building Action Plan for Good and for All.

The five-year plan as engine

Domestically, the push coincides with the launch of the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026–2030. According to Chinese sources, an intelligent economic system is to be built; the core AI industry, diplomatic circles say, has already reached a volume of more than 1.2 trillion yuan.

AI is no longer anything special in China, the narrative goes — it is already widespread, from smart manufacturing to consumer devices. At the same time, laws, regulations, application guidelines, and ethical principles are being continuously developed to keep AI safe and controllable.

China also sees itself as a provider of international public goods, including through the release of open-source models.

Export controls, energy, exchange rates

One sore point in Europe that stands in the way of closer cooperation is China’s export controls on critical minerals needed for semiconductors, batteries, and other key technologies. Beijing rejects the claim that these have caused lasting supply problems, pointing to expedited approval procedures and general licenses for companies. The additional controls, however, are suspended only until No. 10. Whether the relaxations will be extended or stricter licensing requirements will resume afterward remains an open question.

Beijing also pushes back against the recent accusation by Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz that China is keeping the renminbi artificially low. Against the euro, the Chinese currency has in fact risen from around 8.27 to roughly 7.71 yuan per euro since late October — an appreciation of a good seven percent.

The latest currency report from the U.S. Treasury Department, dated July 23, also does not classify China as a currency manipulator. Due to a lack of transparency in its exchange-rate policy, however, the country remains on the U.S. monitoring list. Europe’s criticism of China’s trade surpluses, subsidies, and state-led industrial policy is far from settled.

Despite Merz’s sweeping announcements about resuming German-Chinese government consultations, no date has been set so far. The chancellor had indicated a meeting would take place this year, or early 2027 at the latest. There is, as they say, plenty to discuss.

The author is Alexander Dergay, the founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, a research and analysis firm. Dergay is also cooperating with geopolitical foresight agency Nightingale Int. He worked for several years as an adviser and analyst specializing in geostrategic risk before serving as an foreign policy editor at the Berliner Zeitung and the Ostdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, Germany.
