"Forestry and wood processing matter enormously to Tai Rāwhiti and to the people employed in them. Industry is telling me it faces decisions it considers unworkable and costly, and growing uncertainty about the future of the sector in the region.

"I am advised this is affecting the willingness of investors to pursue processing ventures, both in Tai Rāwhiti and elsewhere in the country."

The forestry industry welcomed the move. New Zealand Forest Owners Association chief executive Dr Elizabeth Heeg said Doug Leeder's appointment provided an opportunity to make progress on difficult questions around land use, woody debris and forestry-related environmental issues.

"Tai Rāwhiti needs to see decision-making that recognises where land use has to change, while allowing forestry to continue on land where it remains appropriate.

"Bringing government, Gisborne District Council, iwi, communities and industry together with an independent facilitator gives us a practical way to work through those issues."

Ngāti Porou Forests chairman Whaimutu Dewes said decisions about land use had long-term consequences for iwi landowners and communities.

"For iwi landowners, there is a responsibility to look after the whenua for generations to come but also to create opportunities for our people on Monday. Forestry supports whānau by generating employment and providing income from whenua to sustain our communities.

"Bringing iwi, communities, government, Council and industry together gives us a better chance of making decisions that achieve both."

Gisborne District Council has been approached for comment.

In 2024, Todd McClay established the Tai Rāwhiti Forestry Action Group (TFAG) to allow the government and council to work closely with the sector to remove slash from the district.

World.title: Another business case for Auckland harbour crossing confirmed despite recent NZTA study
World.content:
The government has announced a detailed business case for a new Waitematā Harbour crossing in Auckland.

That's despite an investment case already having been completed by the Transport Agency (NZTA) - including value engineering and a barge doing seabed testing - just three months ago.

Announcing the new business case at the weekly post-Cabinet briefing on Monday, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said it was unacceptable weight restrictions and a lack of bus lanes were restricting use of the current Harbour bridge.

He said the bridge formed part of the busiest corridor on state highways across the country.

But despite the NZTA's study recommending a tunnel, the ministers said more work was needed before Cabinet could select a preferred option.

A jack-up barge doing seabed testing in the Waitematā harbour last year. Davina Zimmer

"Previous governments have gone out and announced what they are going to build before they have done the work required around how much it will cost, how they are going to pay for it, and whether the project is deliverable. This Government does not intend to make the same mistake," Bishop said.

"We need Auckland - New Zealand's economic engine room - connected, productive, and set up for growth and prosperity. The case for a new crossing is strong, and we are committed to delivering it," Bishop said.

"The WHC (Waitematā Harbour Crossing) project will likely be the largest and most expensive infrastructure project ever undertaken in New Zealand. It is imperative that we get it right because New Zealand's fiscal position, economic performance, and reputation as a modern, functional, first-world country depends on it."

The work would be carried out by an independent "senior responsible officer and completed some time in 2027.

'Study about a study' - Labour

Labour leader Chris Hipkins described the media conference as an "announcement about an announcement about a study about a study".

"They can't make a decision about a decision. These are not serious people. They promised real progress, they haven't delivered."

Bishop indicated Labour's Tangi Utikere had been briefed on the decisions earlier in the morning.

"We're not politicising it. It would have been easy to stand up and announce we're building a bridge or a tunnel, and then everyone would go 'oh, this is very exciting', but we're not doing that ... it's amazing what happens when you do the right thing," Bishop said.

Other than the briefing to Utikere, Hipkins said he had not heard of other bipartisan consultation or discussion on the harbour crossing from National this term but he would need to check.

However, he said Labour would not cancel the government's business case, saying he thought the unanswered questions were what the NZTA investment case had been aimed at solving.

"They've commissioned it, we're not going to stop it ... I thought the detailed business case was what they committed to doing two years ago. They clearly haven't done that. So we'll continue what they have now commissioned.

"One area where I would agree with Christopher Luxon on is there's been way too much flip-flopping and chopping and changing of priorities in this area ... if the National Party was true to its word, it wouldn't have done that itself two and a half years ago or three years ago.

"We've extended a bipartisan spirit to the government on all infrastructure issues through the term of this Parliament. Thus far, on their side, that's involved them saying what they want to do and telling us we should agree with it. That isn't what bipartisanship looks like."

Bishop also said Cabinet had agreed to commission another study into Meola Reef - as backed by Auckland mayor Wayne Brown - if the council was interested, and willing to pay half the Meola study's cost.

The council would be invited to take part in the Meola study.

Ministers would also consider a market-led proposal for an "innovative construction methodology" to upgrade the current Auckland Harbour bridge.

Bishop said NZTA had done good work to get the project to this point but the government believed the project should be directly responsible to ministers.

The SRO would be directly answerable to the Finance, Transport and Auckland Ministers as well as Cabinet, and would be recruited globally to find "someone with the expertise and experience to deliver", he said.

"Every country that has built a megaproject this size has learned the same lesson: they cost more and take longer than the first estimates suggest. Not necessarily because of the engineering, but because of scale, duration, and the number of approvals and decision-makers involved along the way," he said.

"That's a governance problem, and it has a governance solution."

Bishop said the Meola Reef option had been looked at "many times in the past before and discounted as unachievable" but Cabinet had agreed to commission a further study "in the spirit of good faith" if the council desired it.

The proposal to strengthen the existing bridge had come from a "reputable international consortium", and officials had recommended it be advanced and included as part of the detailed business case.

"As Mayor Brown has said, projects don't go wrong - they start wrong. I couldn't agree more, that's why we are making sure we set this project and, by extension, Auckland up for success," Bishop said.

Bishop indicated actual construction would take anywhere between five and nine years, possibly longer.

Tunnel or bridge?

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the government was not set on whether a new crossing would be a tunnel, a bridge or some other option.

"We're saying let's go back, let's look and understand the lay of the land, let's literally get on board the council, let's get on board as many of our bipartisan friends across the aisle that we possibly can and take them with us because we know this will be a long-run project over multiple years, potentially multiple governments, and we want to get that right."

Luxon said John Key's government in 2016 had presented "a lovely A3 glossy picture" of a tunnel, and the last Labour government had done the same, but New Zealand was in the top 10 percent in the OECD for spending and the bottom 10 percent for delivery, asset management and renewal.

"We are genuinely trying to do this differently. You can't just sit in a desk, draw some squiggles over the line, do a bit of an AI artist impression and say we've got a plan," he said.

"We can chuck numbers out there but honestly when it's plus or minus billions of dollars, what's the point ... lots of discussion, lots of debate, lots of AI-generated pictures and we kid ourselves and it's fake activity, nothing's happening - and we've got to get it done."

A visualisation of NZTA's proposed Auckland habour crossings. Supplied

Bishop said the previous investment cases still left unanswered questions including how much it would cost, whether it should be tolled, how it would be delivered, and when it might open.

"Rather than leave those questions unanswered to make a well-informed decision, we're actually going to do international best practice and answer those questions before we make a decision."

That was despite him saying when announcing NZTA's investment case in October 2024 that the report would be a "detailed analysis of the highest-performing bridge and tunnel options".

"They have done that. The board has considered considered both those proposals and their preference is a tunnel ... but they are not the experts in the highly complicated and complex governance structures, management structures, and the funding and financing options to deliver this."

He was "confident" NZTA's work had "significantly advanced" the work towards another harbour crossing but the government needed to know "a lot more" than could be gleaned from desktop studies.

Asked how the government had already spent more than $100m on consultants to scope such projects and those questions remained unanswered, he said that was because it would be "the most expensive and complicated infrastructure project ever in New Zealand history".

The Meola Reef option would be capped at $1m, Luxon said.

Matt Lowrie - the director of the Greater Auckland transport advocacy website - said the problem with an additional harbour crossing had always been the cost.

"NZTA have wanted the biggest most expensive option possible, and that's what's come out of most of the studies that have come out, even though other practical solutions often exist.

"The problem is that they're just never able to be financed."

Lowrie said there needed to be "a bit of reality involved" around what was affordable and practical to build.

"We can't build the most expensive thing, as much as we might like to, we've got to be able to pay for these."

He said the government should not rush to spend billions on a new harbour crossing if there were cheaper alternatives such as congestion charging, where people pay to use the road at certain times.

"Depending on the nature of that scheme, some of the implications are that that would reduce the amount of traffic on the roads and that would extend the life of the existing bridge."

Lowrie said NZTA research showed that with the correct maintenance, the bridge will last indefinitely.

"We shouldn't be rushing to spend billions of dollars if we can have a solution that will solve it for much cheaper."

Lowrie said the government's decision to include a Meola Reef option in the study was about appeasing Mayor Wayne Brown.

"The government are effectively putting the ball in Wayne's court. He has to pay up half the money if he wants to investigate this option further."

World.title: Online radio stations beat the algorithm to cater to some niche tastes
World.content:
[audiio] https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/audio/2019047984/popularity-of-sleep-radio-booms-in-recent-years

Would you like to fall asleep to birdsong or relive the first time you heard your favourite band?

The internet has allowed anyone to start their own station - catering to some niche tastes from era-specific-only music to local gossip.

John Watson, started Sleep Radio in 2012, after being diagnosed with depression from having to make people redundant at his corporate HR job.

"And of course, with depression comes insomnia. And I often get out of bed at night feeling completely awake, go and watch TV until about six in the morning and then be like a zombie for the rest of the day."

He said he tried relaxation CDs - which were difficult to find - and online radios - which would wake him up with adverts or station IDs.

"And I thought, I've got to do something better than this. So I basically created my own playlist."

He said he wondered how many people suffered with insomnia: he found millions through support groups on Facebook.

From there, Watson started a website then launched his own online radio station to share the music that had helped him.

"We had I think about 10 listeners on the first night, and within a week it was over 1000 and I was quite astounded."

A year ago, he did another count and found he had 50,000 regular listeners every month in 190 countries.

Artists and listeners send him music to broadcast as it is difficult to find the right kind.

He told RNZ the music most "conducive to sleep" was ambient, slow, instrumental and wordless.

This was also why the station has a global appeal, he said, and because someone was always trying to sleep somewhere in the world.

The testimonials page on his website showed this best: a commentator in Antarctica said it helped him sleep during six months of daylight.

"Every week, we get fantastic emails and messages from people telling them how it's helped them in their battle with insomnia. And I get a real buzz out of that."

One childcare centre told him they put his station on at naptime.

"I never, ever thought that I would be able to help so many people," Watson said.

80s and 90s only - Nostalgia

Niche radio stations seemed ideally suited for nostalgia: playing the tunes audiences had grown up with.

Bradley "B-Man" Simmons started Keep Laughing Forever Radio, playing only songs from the 80s and 90s, after being diagnosed with myalgic encephalomyelitis chronic fatigue syndrome, which causes debilitating fatigue.

After becoming housebound, he decided to revisit an old dream of becoming a radio DJ, which he had let go of to work at a bank.

"I quickly discovered that peddling term deposits and insurance wasn't quite as rock'n'roll as being a radio DJ."

Bradley "B-Man" Simmons of Keep Laughing Forever Radio. Supplied

He said his goal was to make his listeners nostalgic.

"It was a time before everyone was glued to a screen 24/7, before auto-tune became a thing and before deciding what song to listen to involved scrolling through thousands of options.

"There was something magical about hearing a song come on unexpectedly and thinking, I haven't heard this in years. That feeling is something that I really want to bring back."

Simmonds broadcast music all day and played his shows - Powerzone with Paul Rands, All About The 80s with Rob Charles - which released every fortnight.

He also added jingles, TV themes and movie quotes from that era.

"Those little moments that made radio feel like a friend in your room. Back then radio wasn't just something that you listened to, it was something that made you smile."

His app reached more than 10,000 downloads.

"The response has been amazing," he said.

James McKenzie told RNZ he had been listening to Simmonds' radio station since it began 12 years ago.

"I'm nearly 50 years old and so that era that he is focusing on is totally what I grew up [with] - the 80s and 90s."

He said listening to the show sends him back in time.

"And you think about: 'Oh, what was I doing when I was, you know, 15 years old, when I heard this song for the first time?'"

During the 80s and 90s, he said, there were more cultural touchstones people could bond over, like music.

"You don't go to school and talk about what happened on that episode of Elf or whatever, you know. Because kids have such variety and exposure to so much these days."

And it turned out nostalgia did not only work for those who had lived through the 80s and 90s.

Seventeen-year-old Luka Harrop joined Keep Laughing Forever Radio as the "Gen Rock Guy".

He said his family raised him on music from that time.

"When I was young, in Australia, we went to see Kiss, who have been one of my biggest idols."

He told RNZ being part of the Keep Laughing Forever helped him connect with people who loved the same music he did.

"I suppose it's quite special to me because not too many people my age still listen to it."

He said he liked how upbeat the music was and its counter-cultural, alternative aesthetic.

Being on the radio sparked an interest in a media career, he said.

Keep Laughing Forever Radio has been broadcast in more than 30 stations around the world, including on Retro Hit Radio in Auckland, which also only played songs from the 80s and 90s.

Richard Phelps has been running the station for more than two decades.

He said his radio station featured the "uniquely Kiwi flavour" New Zealand artists brought to the genre, which he believed had been overlooked by mainstream radio at the time.

"So we had a really unique blend of music and that's not replicated anywhere these days," he said.

He described the Dunedin music scene in the 80s and 90s as "rock heavy, it's a little punky, it's a little alternative".

He said online radio stations could give audiences more than an algorithm: they offered story-telling and connection.

World.title: Urgent care clinic absorbing patients from crowded ED
World.content:
A 24/7 urgent care clinic in South Auckland is absorbing patients from the local hospital's crowded emergency department as EDs around the country hit peak winter demand.

The waiting room is often crowded at Local Doctors Otara, and more patients are now coming through the door, with another local South Auckland clinic temporarily closing due to staffing issues and sickness.

Local Doctors Otara started operating 24/7 this year to meet growing demand, and says patients have been coming to them to avoid long waits at Middlemore Hospital.

Urgent care clinic absorbing patients from hospitals Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Doctor Niroshika Kotte Arachchige said wait times at Urgent Care had been up to five hours during the winter peak.

"This winter the flu season has been particularly severe. We are seeing a higher number of sick children, elderly patients, coming to our service throughout the day."

Young mother Amber-Lee Moutira brought in her baby to check out a nasty sounding cough.

"My 8-month-old baby started experiencing some flu-like, almost RSV-like symptoms and I've had a past history with experiencing RSV symptoms with my first son."

Moutira was seeing the winter peak first hand - her whole family was sick at the moment.

"It can feel back to back, just one after the other, and then when everyone gets better again, boom it starts again."

She was still waiting to see a doctor when she talked to RNZ, and said she had waited several hours at the clinic in the past.

She said the house she and her family lived in was old, and got cold and damp in the winter, which did not help her children's health.

"Especially my son's room where mould grows on the blinds, and the curtains. I've tried so many ways and the whole vinegar buzz just spraying it all the time to kill the bacteria. But I've noticed it just really sparks out during the winter time and I notice it in my bathroom."

Waiting room at Local Doctors Otara about 9:30am. RNZ / Luka Forman

Dr Kotte Arachchige said many patients were sent to their clinic from Middlemore, some after already spending hours waiting at the hospital.

"Sometimes some patients have waited all night and they come and see us the next day... because they have staffing issues at night also and only a few doctors working."

She said others were coming to the clinic to avoid a two to three week wait to see a GP.

RNZ understands another urgent care clinic in South Auckland - Counties Medical Urgent Care Takanini - has had to shut temporarily due to staff sickness and shortages.

Doctor Kotte Arachchige said those patients were also ending up at her clinic.

"We see patients from everywhere, we see casual patients.. patients from other urgent care... basically demand is so high here."

Dr Kotte Arachchige said stable and sustainable funding was needed to keep the clinic going 24 hours, seven days a week.

"So the funding is not just about keeping the clinic open, it is an investment in community care and reducing the pressure on the wider system as well."

Clinic community manager Liamanaia Kaisara said the community was grateful to have the clinic open 24/7.

"They are able to come anytime to the urgent service here, in your own backyard and it is the first one here, in South Auckland."

World.title: Pauline Hanna 'impaired but not incapacitated' - pharmacologist
World.content:
A pharmacologist has suggested Auckland health manager Pauline Hanna was impaired, but not incapacitated or unconscious, the night before she was found dead in her Remuera home.

Her husband Philip Polkinghorne was acquitted of her murder in 2024.

Now a coronial inquest is underway, with Coroner Tania Tetitaha attempting to determine how Hanna died and the circumstances surrounding her death.

At the Coroner's Court in Auckland on Monday, Emeritus Professor Macdonald Christie said Hanna's blood alcohol level at or close to the time of her death was well below the legal driving limit for an adult.

But the pharmacologist said her urine alcohol concentration was higher, suggesting she was intoxicated in the hours prior to her death.

Polkinghorne has previously said Hanna went to her bedroom alone after 10pm on 4 April 2021, and that was the last time he saw her alive.

Giving evidence at the inquest last week, he told the coroner his wife drank one-and-a-half bottles of wine that night.

Zopiclone, a sleeping medication, which she was not prescribed, was also found in her system. Christie said it was very likely she took more than one zopiclone tablet that night, but it was hard to say exactly when.

During her cross-examination, Police Counsel Alysha McClintock asked what Hanna's state might have been if she did consume that amount of alcohol, along with zopiclone.

Christie said he would expect her to experience issues with "balance and gait", "thinking coherently" and "difficulty rousing from sleep". But he said Hanna was not at the point where she could not be woken.

He clarified to Polkinghorne's lawyer, Ron Mansfield, during his cross-examination that she would still respond to a "strong physical stimulus".

"Certainly, if she was touched or shaken, that would be sufficient to wake her, correct?" Mansfield said.

"Yes, that's likely," Christie responded.

"[Zopiclone] hastens and prolongs sleep. The goal of the drug, which it largely succeeds in doing, is to produce as normal as possible a 'sleep state', of which normally we are rousable."

Philip Polkinghorne. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Mansfield asked if Hanna would be coherent enough to fight back if an argument occurred, as McClintock had suggested earlier in the inquest.

"Certainly around the time of death, she could engage in a physical altercation and/or seek to defend herself?" Mansfield asked.

"I would believe so, yes, in some manner," said Christie.

Christie said it was hard to determine exactly how impaired Hanna was as this would depend on how much tolerance she had to both alcohol and zopiclone.

But he said that because of Hanna's low blood alcohol level when she died, if she did drink more than a bottle of wine that night, it was extremely unlikely she died before 1am on 5 April.

He said levels of phentermine - a weight-loss drug - and amoxapine, an antidepressant which she was prescribed, also found in her system were within therapeutic levels.

But he confirmed, when asked by McClintock, no methamphetamine was found in her system at the time of her death.

Polkinghorne has denied throughout the inquest that traces of meth found by police in his wife's bathroom were his.

Much of what was discussed at the inquest on Monday was relating to a possible cause of Hanna's death, which cannot be reported on.

World.title: Golf course in court as parklands protesters take on SA government
World.content:
In what's been described as a David and Goliath battle, a trial has begun in the Federal Court, with two South Australians challenging the state government's redevelopment of the North Adelaide golf course.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera are challenging the redevelopment, arguing it is in breach of federal conservation laws.

In front of other protesters opposed to the parklands project outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said the unfolding legal process was "very nerve-wracking".

"It's a big uphill battle for us but we're really proud to be standing here," he said.

Ms Milera said she was taking action because she thought it was the right thing to do.

"This case is about respecting cultural tradition and truth telling," she said.

For [SA Premier] Peter [Malinauskas], it's a new golf course. For me, it's a bloodline.

"This case we're doing is because the parklands belong to the people and they need to be protected."

Protesters opposed to the state government's actions in the Adelaide parklands gathered outside the Federal Court. (ABC News: Leah MacLennan)

The state government announced its plan to redevelop and expand the golf course, as part of its bid to move the LIV Golf tournament into the city.

It said 585 trees would be cut down in the process, to be replaced with new plantings.

The state government passed laws earlier this year, taking control of that part of the parklands away from the Adelaide City Council, to allow it to go ahead with the redevelopment.

But the removal of trees sparked protests and the legal action taken by Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera.

The redevelopment of the North Adelaide course has involved the felling of hundreds of trees. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

In his opening address, the lawyer for the pair, Arturo Dal Cin, told the court the Adelaide parklands were given national heritage listing in 2008.

He said more than 400 trees had already cut down at the golf course — a number he said accounted for 15 per cent of all the trees in the area marked for the first stage of the development.

"Recognition of parklands necessarily includes recognition of established trees, because a necessary element of parklands is established, mature trees," Mr Dal Cin said.

He said the works have impacted the national heritage values of the parklands.

"A fundamental issue in this case, one of the fundamental issues, is the extent to which your Honour finds the removal of trees to this scale to be a significant impact on what the appellants will be contending is a national heritage value — namely the parklands and their protection," he said.

Trees were removed from the area in May. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Dal Cin said evidence would also be presented during the trial about the impact on Aboriginal cultural heritage and on local flying fox populations.

'Assault on democracy'

Before going to court, government lawyers wrote to Mr Kemp Attrill, warning him he could be liable for $4 million in costs if he lost.

Outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said the government had not backed down.

"It's really concerning to us that in a public interest case the government has continued to say that they will essentially crush us if they win," he said.

"We think that's incredibly unfair and it's an assault on democracy in South Australia."

Mr Kemp Attrill had submitted an affidavit to the court saying he was "shocked" when he saw the loss of trees.

On cross-examination, he was shown aerial pictures of the course before and after the tree removal.

Crown lawyer Alison Doecke KC asked if a significant number of trees remained in the parklands following the works.

"I put to you that when one has regard to the aerial view, it is very hard to identify where the trees have been removed," she said.

"From the two photographs, yes," Mr Kemp Attrill said.

He said he often walks his dog around the golf course at night, and he has noticed the loss of trees.

"Walking around the perimeter, you can notice there's more sky," he said.

The redevelopment of the course was announced as part of plans for LIV Golf. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Ms Doecke suggested to Mr Kemp Attrill that "the significant change in the appearance of the site is because of the removal of the grass, not the removal of the trees. Do you accept that?" she said.

"No, as I said, it was noticeable as soon as the trees were removed; the view was different," Mr Kemp Attrill said.

"Standing outside the fence, if you're not right up against the fence you actually don't see the grass, you can only see the trees, and that was a noticeable difference."

But when asked by Ms Doecke if he would concede "there's still an awful lot of trees on the site", Mr Kemp Attrill said "yes".

Speaking at a media conference, Premier Peter Malinauskas said his government has acted lawfully.

"All the advice that I've received from the relevant agencies is they've sought to comply with all requirements as they've gone through it," he said.

" I've said all along that any individual is welcome to take up their rights to challenge things in court, as is being done in this particular instance. "

The trial is expected to take five days, with government lawyers to present their response on Wednesday.

World.title: Sydney Swans CEO confirms police investigating alleged incident 'involving several players'
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have confirmed several of their footballers were involved in an "alleged incident" in Melbourne last night.

The Swans issued a statement just after midday today.

"The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage," the club said.

Victoria Police separately issued a statement saying detectives were investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne.

The Sydney Swans stayed at the Pullman in East Melbourne last night. (ABC News)

"The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning," a spokesperson said.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established, and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing."

Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich called a press conference this afternoon that lasted less than one minute.

"We're still piecing together exactly what's transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing," he said.

"Safe to say, we're extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation.

"We understand the level of interest in the matter, and there's going to be lots of speculation, but given it's a police matter right now, that's all that we can say."

Matthew Pavlich addressed the media this afternoon. (ABC News)

The AFL released a brief statement.

"The club made the AFL aware of the matter which is currently under Victoria Police investigation," the statement read.

NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said she was unaware of the details of the allegations, but she was confident Victorian authorities would take them "very seriously."

"We have to be mindful of the fact that the alleged offences occurred in a different jurisdiction. So, they [Victoria Police] will be leading that investigation," she said.

Asked if she would be seeking a briefing from police herself given it was a high-profile case allegedly involving Sydney-based AFL players, she said: "The police will definitely lead on that" and "brief me accordingly".

"The investigation is underway, I think we should let the police do their work in Victoria, and the NSW police will let me know if I need to know anything."

The Swans were staying in Melbourne overnight after their 36-point win over Essendon at the MCG yesterday.

Sydney is sitting in second spot on the AFL ladder heading into the final round of the 2026 season, with the finals due to start within weeks.

The team has had 17 wins this season and is due to play its next game at home at the SCG against North Melbourne.

World.title: No smiles as Chris O'Connell advances, while Aussie women's campaign ends
World.content:
Chris O'Connell and Adam Walton have made it four Australian men in the third round of the Cincinnati Master, while Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka left the women's draw without green and gold representation.

Gibson was beaten 6-2, 7-6(7/2) by the world number one in an hour and 52 minutes, while O'Connell and Walton joined Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata in the round of 32.

But O'Connell was in no mood to celebrate after progressing thanks to an injury retirement by 11th-seeded opponent Casper Ruud.

The Australian qualifier picked up his fourth win in five days at the Masters 1000 tournament in what is proving his most profitable week of the season, but there were no smiles as he sympathised with Norway's three-time grand slam finalist on his concerning retirement after 64 minutes play.

Ruud had started well, moving into a 5-2 lead in the opening set, but the Sydneysider powered back to take the first set, sealing it 7-5 with an ace, as Ruud began to look in increasing discomfort with a back problem.

With Ruud leading the second set 2-1 on serve, the Norwegian world number 17 stretched for a wide serve and immediately decided enough was enough, going to the net to offer his hand to the Aussie.

Clearly with one eye on the US Open, where the main draw starts a week on Sunday, 2022 Flushing Meadows runner-up Ruud was not keen to take any risks.

For world number 129 O'Connell, it was the continuation of an excellent spell following his first-round victory over Poland's world number 68 Kamil Majchrzak.

He will next meet Brazilian teenage superstar Joao Fonseca, who defeated Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-6(7/2), and victory in that match would push O'Connell back to the verge of the world's top 100.

Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka leaves no Australian women in the Cincinnati singles draw. (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Walton made it four Australians through to the third round along with Hijikata, who faces Jakub Mensik, and national number one Alex de Minaur, who meets British Wimbledon hero Arthur Fery.

Walton, the 27-year-old Queenslander currently ranked 98 in the world, overcame the 29th-seeded Peruvian Ignacio Buse 6-4, 6-3 in 72 minutes to set up a showdown with either American Ben Shelton, the eighth seed, or Jaime Faria of Portugal.

World.title: After constant chopping and changing, Green goes 'back to what worked'
World.content:
Cameron Green has delivered for a shell-shocked Australian side to give himself breathing space at number five, leading captain Pat Cummins to predict a long stint in one position in the batting line-up.

Green's 104 in the second innings of the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin was his first in Australia and also broke an 11-innings run without passing the half-century mark.

The 27-year-old all-rounder has been heavily criticised in Australian cricket for not turning his undoubted potential into results.

But his knock in the loss means he leaves the Northern Territory as one of the only Aussie batters who can hold their heads high, with Cummins "not too sure" on the best course of action to turn things around before the second Test starts in Mackay on Saturday.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

"We're always quite individual, everyone goes about it slightly differently, so coaches will work with each player individually," he said.

"I don't think there was a huge trend, everyone got out a little bit differently, but I think it's pretty clear it's not quite functioning as well as we'd like as a group.

"If we need to make some changes to our style, we've got a week or so, we better do it pretty quickly."

Cummins said before the Test that Green had been encouraged to "intimidate" and he did it the way he knows best, driving with commanding power and poise while accumulating runs at a steady rate without taking risks.

It is a method that has worked in Sheffield Shield cricket and he showcased why Test selectors have persevered with him despite the outside noise calling for his head.

Green's third Test century did not lead to a win but that was largely due to the failure of the rest of the order to stay with him in good batting conditions on the third and fourth days.

Australia will consider making changes to the underperforming top order for the second Test in Mackay that starts on Saturday, but Green will be one of the first picked.

"I'm sure he will get an extended run somewhere," Cummins said when asked if Green had tied down the number five position.

"I thought he was really impressive and controlled his innings. He looked in total command of his skills out there. He just needed one or two of us to bat alongside him."

Green and Steve Smith were the only Australian batters who could be happy with their output. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green struggled in the last Ashes series, as many batters did, making just 171 runs at an average of 24.42 after being moved around from fifth to eighth in the order.

He earlier did a solid job on the West Indies tour, averaging 30.66 at first drop as the only member of the top three to average more than 20 across the three Tests.

"We obviously think very highly of Cam," Cummins said.

"The last Ashes series probably didn't go as well as he would have liked but before that on the West Indian tour he was probably our best batter in really tough circumstances when he was batting a little higher.

"It was great for him to go out there and show the rest of the world how good he is."

Quick hits as Bangladesh wraps up famous win Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them. Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

Green was fortunate in the final session on the third day when an inside edge off Taskin Ahmed grazed his leg stump on the way to the boundary.

The bails were not dislodged and the all-rounder dug in and made the most of his reprieve.

Green told Fox Cricket after his knock that he had approached his innings against Bangladesh like he used to do "back in the day".

"I think I've just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so it's nice just to go back to what worked," Green said.

"It has been a long couple of months so it is nice to get a few rewards for it."

As for the critics, Green said it just came with the territory.

"I feel like there are always wolves when you are playing Test cricket. When you play for Australia, you always have to perform," he said.

World.title: Aussie star Lani Pallister ends American GOAT's 16-year win streak
World.content:
Lani Pallister has toppled swimming legend Katie Ledecky for a second time in 24 hours to complete her stunning Pan Pacific championship campaign with a fourth gold medal.

The 24-year-old Pallister was under world-record pace for much of the race as she won the 800m freestyle final in eight minutes and 6.1 seconds from four-time Olympic champion Ledecky (8:07.26) in the American's signature event.

Ledecky's lone previous defeat in an 800m freestyle final since 2010 came in a small domestic event in February 2024 against Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh, making Pallister the first to beat her over the distance at an international meet.

"Today is the most nervous I've ever felt in my entire life. I was just so locked in and I've been really focused on what I want," Pallister said.

"The 800m is my favourite event. So to have the three titles this week and be just behind Katie in the 1,500 [is great but] … this is the one that I wanted."

Ledecky, who famously signed an autograph for a young Pallister a decade ago, telling her to "dream big", wrote on Instagram that she "can't help but smile about another incredible race with [Pallister]".

Ledecky (right) told a young Pallister to "dream big". (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Pallister had beaten Ledecky to win the 400m freestyle gold a day earlier and took silver behind her great rival in the 1,500m free, as well as downed McIntosh to win the 200m free gold and also collect gold in the 4x200m free relay.

Australia's Dolphins well and truly flexed their middle- and long-distance muscle at the meet, two years out from the LA Olympics, with Sam Short also emerging with three individual gold medals after winning the men's 1,500m free to go with his 400 and 800 free titles.

Having beaten Ian Thorpe's 1999 Pan Pacs record to win the 400m, he erased another Australian legend's mark in the 1,500m.

His time of 14:33.97 was the sixth-fastest in history, breaking Grant Hackett's Australian record that had stood since 2001, and came a day after German teenager Johannes Liebmann smashed the world record at the European Aquatics Championships.

Loading Instagram content

"I am proud of my consistency," said Short, who also won the 400m, 800m, and 1,500m titles at the Commonwealth Games late last month.

"I've gone five well sub-15-minute swims now, so if I can do that here my average come Olympics, world championships, all I need to do is be my average and be contending for some podium places."

Adding to a strong final day for Australia, Zac Stubblety-Cook went from fourth to first in the 200m breaststroke final, winning in 2:08.09 from American Josh Matheny.

And countryman Jamie Jack won the 50m freestyle gold in a championship record of 21.35 as American Jack Alexy took silver in 21.42.

"It's awesome. That's the best I could ask for," Jack said.

American Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the 50m free twice, winning the final in 23.19.

Douglass capped a busy night by anchoring the US women to a dominant victory in the 4x100 medley relay in a championship record time of 3:50.43, with Australia second in 3:55.09.

The US men won from Australia in the 4x100 medley relay.

Australia finished the four-day meet with a medal haul of 15 gold, 11 silver and nine bronze, behind only the US haul of 19, 22 and nine.

World.title: Off-grid stories during F1 mid-year break as racing returns
World.content:
Formula 1's mid-year hiatus ends this weekend, as the racing series returns to action with the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort.

The five-week break has given drivers and teams a chance to refresh ahead of a long and gruelling run to the finish line, with the drivers' and constructors' championships well and truly alive in 2026.

While there has been no action on the track, there has been news off it during the break.

Ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, here are a few stories you may have missed during the hiatus.

1. No contract announcements

The first news is no news.

Drivers off contract at the end of 2026 Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

George Russell, Mercedes

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull

Carlos Sainz, Williams

Alex Albon, Williams

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin

Oliver Bearman, Haas

Esteban Ocon, Haas

Nick Hulkenberg, Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi

Franco Colapinto, Alpine

The mid-year break usually signals the start of F1's silly season, where teams and drivers formalise contracts for future seasons.

The 2026 silly season is set to be busy, with as many as 14 drivers off contract at the end of this year.

And there are big names who are yet to finalise deals for 2027 and beyond, including Mercedes drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli, and two-time world champion Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin).

There has also been wild speculation of a potential driver swap between McLaren and Red Bull, with Australia's Oscar Piastri and four-time world champion Max Verstappen changing teams as early as next year.

But, thus far, there have been no announcements.

This will change in the near future, and just because no contracts have been announced does not mean no work behind the scenes.

2. Piastri confident McLaren can 'make that step' back to the top

After the highs of the previous two seasons, McLaren's 2026 campaign has resembled more of a yo-yo.

McLaren have won the previous two constructors' championships, while Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri both won seven grands prix last year, a campaign where Norris became drivers' world champion.

Piastri blasts 'f***ing stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP Oscar Piastri retired from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, won by his teammate Lando Norris, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

But in 2026, with a new era of regulations, McLaren has had mixed results.

It started the season poorly, with Oscar Piastri failing to start the opening two grands prix of the season (Australia and China), while Norris also failed to start the Chinese Grand Prix.

Both drivers have been plagued by reliability issues, but have also produced promising results.

Piastri has twice finished on the podium (Japan and Miami), while Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix — a race Piastri led before being hit by a backmarker and then suffering an issue that forced his retirement.

Despite not being in the championship picture thus far in 2026, Piastri is confident McLaren will return.

In an interview with the team during the break, Piastri cited McLaren's early struggles in 2023 before their rise up the grid to become back-to-back champions.

"When you look at the previous experience of what we've been able to achieve as a team, and how we've been able to make progress through the year, it's good," the Australian said.

"In 2023, we were in a much worse position than where we are now, and we were able to really jump up the order to fight for podiums.

"The way that Lando and I worked together during that period to try and focus on making the car quick, so that we could then fight for the results that we wanted, hasn't changed. It's still strong, with productive conversations together with the team — we are all pushing toward the same goal.

"I feel like for me I've already seen it play out more than once. I think that's a real strength of the team. Yes, things are different, the cars are different, maybe the way we will make that step will look different. But we've made that step before, and I'm confident we can do it again."

3. Bahrain Grand Prix back on calendar, in Malaysia

While the official mid-year break is coming to an end, F1 had an unofficial hiatus earlier this year when the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia weekends were called off due to unrest in the Middle East.

That left an unexpected gap between the Japanese Grand Prix and Miami Grand Prix weekends, with F1 holding onto hope that they would be able to bring those races back onto the calendar.

Well, they have brought one back, in a different country.

The Bahrain Grand Prix will be held in 2026, but thousands of kilometres away in Malaysia.

Sepang International Circuit will host the event from October 2-4, between the grand prix weekends in Azerbaijan and Singapore.

F1 is no stranger to Sepang, first racing there in 1999, while the last F1 race held there in 2017 was won by Max Verstappen.

"We are delighted to confirm that Malaysia will host the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2026. Once again, the sport has demonstrated its ability to adapt, find solutions, and deliver, creating an exciting moment for everyone who follows Formula 1," F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said.

4. Cadillac has a team principal change

While there was no change in the driver market, F1's newest team made a change on the pit wall.

Cadillac announced Marcin Budkowski would become the American squad's new team principal, replacing Graeme Lowdon.

Lowdon was the team principal from 2024 and an instrumental figure in preparing Cadillac for its debut season in 2026.

Budkowski has been around F1 for many years, and was once the executive director at French outfit Alpine.

"Marcin's appointment marks another important step in the continued evolution of the Cadillac Formula 1 Team," said Dan Towriss, CEO of the Cadillac team.

"As we enter this new era for the Cadillac Formula 1 Team, Marcin brings exceptional F1 experience, technical expertise and strategic leadership that will strengthen our organisation and help us develop the winning mindset, tools and processes required for long-term success.

"We're grateful to Graeme Lowdon for his leadership and the role he played in forming the Cadillac Formula 1 Team from the ground up. His contributions helped establish a strong foundation in our build-up phase, and we thank him for his commitment and wish him well."

World.title: Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight
World.content:
You could pick a handful of moments during the first Test at Marrara Oval in Darwin where it was clear not everything was as it seemed on surface level.

On day two, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted off with his usual exuberance from the infield to chase down a shot that trickled towards the boundary.

The immaculately manicured outfield, offering a playing surface that was nigh on pristine, had already been praised for its lawn-like quality.

Mark Waugh on Fox Sports noted you could probably play bowls or tennis on it.

Yet as soon as Labuschagne slid for the ball, the ugly truth was revealed, as a huge clump of turf was ripped up in a heaped mass of mud and grass and injury potential.

This was a pattern repeated throughout the match: The outfield's undoubted beauty was only surface deep.

Australia's standing at the top of the Test match rankings may only be surface deep, as deep fissures have been revealed in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

An analogy to what transpired over the next four days, as the number nine-ranked Test team that were missing two of their best bowlers, thumped the world number one side at full strength on their own turf, could not have been clearer.

Bangladesh's stunning victory in Darwin has delivered Australian cricket the shock that it undoubtedly needed.

A team that arrived without fanfare or pedigree has slapped down the world's number one Test playing nation by playing simple, sensible Test cricket.

The bowling was slow but accurate. The batting, unspectacular but patient and disciplined.

The Tigers' attitude was exceptional.

As the growth of the big three has accelerated inequalities between the haves and have-nots of Test cricket, Bangladesh are one of those teams that have been left firmly on the outer, yet proved in Darwin that the paucity of opportunities that have come their way has in no way blunted their potency or hunger for success within the format.

They were here to play Test cricket and play it well.

Najmul Hossain Shanto led his team with skill and composure throughout. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Given it had been 23 years since they last played a Test on Australian soil, their commitment to playing such an impressive style against a country that has snubbed them for so long was more than admirable.

Credit for that has to go to coach Phil Simmons and unflappable skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto.

Shanto made correct decision after correct decision on the pitch, Bangladesh never succumbing to the pressure or enormity of what was transpiring around them right up until Mominul Haque crushed Beau Webster through the covers to seal victory, a simple hug between the two not out batters sufficing as the bench finally exploded in joy on the boundary.

Bangladesh's historic win deserves all the praise that will undoubtedly be heaped upon it, the context of which will forever be extraordinary.

Bangladesh held their nerve throughout a tense contest. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Legendary English cricket writer Neville Cardus once wrote that to properly consider Test cricket, you need to see the big picture.

"I wish to present the Test matches in their setting," he wrote in the introduction to his book chronicling the 1936/37 Ashes series.

"To me cricket must be put against a background."

So what is the background here for Australia?

Australia is about to embark on as busy a Test match year as they have ever had, playing as many as 20 Tests in the next 12 months.

From the Top End, the men's Test team will head to South Africa, play New Zealand and England at home, then face overseas tours to India and England for the Ashes in 2027.

It is a demanding schedule both as physically gruelling and mentally taxing as they come.

Steve Smith and Australia have a lot of thinking to do ahead of the next Test. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Starting off with a two-Test series against Bangladesh, a country Australia has only deigned to host once before for a Test series and only played against in red ball cricket six times in total before this week was considered by most to be a friendly warm up, a competitive practice during a winter sojourn in the Top End sun.

It is, of course, incredibly admirable Cricket Australia is taking Test matches to regions that cannot ever hope to host an Ashes contest.

For financial reasons as much as from a societal responsibility, playing these sorts of Tests in this continent's more remote, northern reaches is undoubtedly the right thing to do.

But maybe there is a sense that this is considered a form of benevolence to the lesser-populated areas of the nation.

Perhaps, for some, even playing Bangladesh is a form of charity to a nation that simply does not have the financial pull of the major nations, little more than an obligation to the World Test Championship.

Maybe, despite protestations to the contrary, that attitude sneaks into the minds of the players, so subliminally that they themselves do not even notice it.

Pat Cummins defended the team's preparation, but perhaps they didn't even realise they were underdone. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

For how can playing in front of about 5,000 spectators in a venue where only half the oval is bordered by a grandstand compare with the cathedral-like cavernous majesty of the MCG, or the lack of pressure contrast with the parochial furnace of a packed Gabba?

Marrara Oval offers neither the stately splendour of the Adelaide Oval or SCG, nor the admittedly under-populated grandiosity of the new Perth Stadium.

Darwin is definitively off-Broadway.

And although Australia's defeat didn't seem to be for lack of effort, the application and necessary quality was lacking throughout the match.

Horror drops from Steve Smith and Nathan Lyon were surely aberrations, but the lazy stroke play and jittery, muddled thinking of the batters was very not.

Steve Smith was not his usual best in the field. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This shock to a team that has been creaking under the weight of their own success for a number of years now is one that has probably arrived eight months too late.

It was due last summer against England before those Bazballers tripped up over their own hubris.

A papering of the cracks was the result of that emphatic 4-1 Ashes victory, the foundations of sand upon which the top order was built were never tested, the supposedly seismic impact of a fired up England bowling attack never coming to bare, self-sabotaging itself amidst a storm of recriminations in the boozy sand of Noosa.

So on we continued. Australia's brittle batters went off to earn their coin in meaningly limited overs matches and failed to address the issues that have plagued them in red ball cricket, perhaps even accentuating the problems by promoting angled bats and rash shots.

Now the show moves to Mackay and presents Australia with an ever-bigger list of questions and problems to face.

Jake Weatherald's status as opener has to be looked at. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia were rusty and not up to speed in Darwin.

Even if Mackay's Harrup Park, the newest venue to host a men's Test in Australia, provides a suitably refreshed outlook and attitude from Australia next Saturday, will victory there do anything else other than to plaster even more paper over gaps that are swiftly turning into chasms?

It's been eight years since a rambunctious tour almost boiled over, a sorry spectacle that was quickly overshadowed by a sandpaper-scraping that was barely as coarse as the friction generated by two teams flirting on the edge of respectability throughout.

Any weakness in Australia's psyche will be ripe for exploitation in southern Africa, and the venom is unlikely to be as hidden as it was in the far north of Australia.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

Tech.title: Apple ordered to stop scaring iPhone and iPad users away from third-party apps
Tech.content: In its preliminary assessment, the Bundeskartellamt considered that the current design of the [App Tracking Transparency] prompt steers users towards refusing consent, whereas the design of the [Personalized Ads] prompt steers them towards giving their consent to the use of their data for advertising purposes. Factors that contribute to this steering effect include the symbols used (for example, a warning hand symbol), different wordings (“app tracking” versus “personalised advertising”), partially ambiguous descriptions of how the data will be used, differences in the space available to explain the advantages of allowing data use, and the order in which the selection options are displayed.

Tech.title: WiiM’s capable HomePod-esque smart speaker is almost $50 off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The smart speaker market is more or less dominated by major tech companies: Apple, Google, Sonos, and Amazon. But WiiM’s powerful 100W Sound smart speaker is an attractive alternative because it’s not locked down to play nicely with select music services. It supports over 20 services, and it sports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3 and ethernet, giving you multiple ways to connect. Additionally, it taps into standards used by other speakers, including Chromecast, Spotify Connect, DLNA, Alexa Cast, and more (AirPlay 2 is off the table, though its Pro Music Streamer supports it). In other words, it can be added to multi-room setups you may already have in the Google Home or Amazon Echo ecosystem.

The black and white versions are rarely discounted, but they’re each 15 percent off at Amazon and directly through WiiM. Normally $299.99, they’re $254.15.

WiiM also makes the Sound Lite, which is also discounted by 15 percent. Originally $229, it’s $194.65 at Amazon and WiiM. It has the same dimensions, connectivity and performance output as the Sound (plus, the ability to use AI to adapt its sound quality to your room), but it lacks the 1.8-inch touch display that can show off album art, and there’s no voice remote included — those are around $33. That said, you can wirelessly pair these speakers and other recent WiiM products to each other to build a surround sound setup. Read more in our coverage.

Other great Verge-approved deals

Apple’s AirPods Max 2 over-ear, noise-canceling headphones are down to $429 at All colors ofare down to $429 at Best Buy as part of its 60-year anniversary sale. Originally $549, this sale brings them down to their second-best price, only bested by Prime Day’s $399 deal. Amazon has fewer colors available at this price. In our review , John Higgins praised their improved sound quality and noise cancellation effect, but wished certain things about it had changed. At their original price, he would have liked a proper carrying case included with purchase. But, at least with this discount, you can get a nicer case with the cash you’ll save.

58-inch Hisense 4K QLED Roku TV that’ll do. Normally $399.99, the QD5 is down to $189.99 at Look, sometimes you just need a cheap TV, not an amazing one. If that’s you, there might be athat’ll do. Normally $399.99, the QD5 is down to $189.99 at Best Buy . It doesn’t seem particularly impressive, but it’s a feature-packed TV at a good price. Beyond having built-in Roku guts for streaming movies and TV shows, it supports Dolby Vision, HDR 10 and HLG, and its game mode supports variable refresh rate and auto low latency mode (though, it tops out at 60Hz refresh rate).

Godox ES45 key light recently, and the deal is back on at We highlighted a deal on therecently, and the deal is back on at Amazon . The $20 off sale brings the powerful key light setup down to $119, and while it doesn’t match Elgato’s Key Light one-for-one with specs, it’s a great value that costs $60 less. It has adjustable color temperature and brightness, and its settings can be easily tweaked with its controller, which gets recharged by sticking magnetically to the back of the light. A key light is great for adding a strong light source to your room. It can be used to light you directly, or aim it at the wall to be softly illuminated in light that bounces off.

Tech.title: Uber partners with Zipline on Eats drone deliveries
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Uber is teaming up with drone company Zipline to start airborne takeout deliveries later this year, with the goal of reaching one million daily drone deliveries by 2029.

Uber also said it was making a strategic investment in Zipline, a California-based company that has been orchestrating drone deliveries in Texas since 2025. The news comes as Uber’s delivery rivals begin to step up their own drone deliveries, thanks to easing government regulations that allow companies to fly farther and cheaper.

The Uber Eats deliveries will start in Zipline’s existing market of Dallas-Fort Worth, before eventually expanding to dozens of additional cities. Zipline, which has made two million deliveries so far, also operates overseas, including Rwanda, Ghana, Japan, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, and Kenya. The company first started operations in Rwanda in 2016, delivering medical supplies in minutes to remote locations. The deal is similar to one Uber made with drone company Flytrex last year, which also included an investment by the ridehail giant.

Uber says that Zipline’s drones can bring a customer’s order to their front lawn in a “matter of minutes.” The company claims it is building the world’s largest hybrid network of human couriers, sidewalk robots, and drones, in which customers are matched with the best, most efficient method of delivery, depending on where they live.

But while Uber partners with third-party drone operators, its rivals are seeking regulator approval to deploy their own drones. Last month, DoorDash launched its own drone delivery program called DoorDash Air, after receiving approval from the Federal Aviation Administration.

Thanks to a 2025 order from President Donald Trump, the FAA has proposed new rules to expand the deployment of drone delivery operations. As such, drone operators are scrambling to secure partnerships with grocery chains and major retailers in the hopes of claiming their share of what could be $7.7 billion market by 2031, according to one analysis.

Tech.title: It’s about ethics in journalism, with Ben Smith
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today I’m talking to Ben Smith, the editor-in-chief of Semafor.

Everywhere you go, people say they don’t trust the media — and yet they’ve never consumed more of it. Audiences have moved on from legacy names in favor of Substacks and podcasts and TikTok news influencers that seem to be everywhere in our feeds.

Why would anyone want to start a new global news organization in the middle of all that, when even once-storied brands like CBS News can’t seem to figure it out?

Well, that’s what Ben did four years ago. He’s the guy who ran BuzzFeed News at the height of the Facebook traffic boom, and even wrote a book about it, called Traffic, which he discussed with me on Decoder back in 2023.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Around that same time, he cofounded Semafor, which launched in 2022 with a stated goal of reaching 200 million college-educated readers.

You’re going to hear Ben say that since then, Semafor has evolved into what he calls an anti-scale company. It still doesn’t have a website paywall, but it makes about half its money in the convening business — that’s what media types have taken to calling events lately.

And Semafor throws some big events. It actually has a new one called Silicon Valley & The World, which will feature some of the biggest names in tech and AI. That’s part of the events business: hosting the subjects you cover on your big event stage.

So I wanted to know how that all works, and what it feels like to navigate the ethical conflicts that seem to be everywhere in media right now. In particular, I wanted to dig into how Semafor’s newsroom is approaching AI, the ethics and optics of putting people you cover on your conference advisory boards, and whether independence is still something an audience is willing to pay for.

Ben and I usually hash this stuff out over beers, and I think you can tell we really enjoy getting into all this together.

Okay: Semafor editor-in-chief Ben Smith. Here we go.

This transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Ben Smith, you’re the co-founder and editor in chief of Semafor. Welcome back to Decoder.

It is really nice to be back.

I’m excited to talk to you. You were on the show three years ago, just as Semafor was launching. It was right as Buzzfeed News, which you founded and ran for a long time, was shutting down.

I keep talking to media CEOs about what is going to happen. It feels like you have figured something out at Semafor. How are things going over there?

Things are going incredibly well, and knock on wood as I say that, but I think we figured something out. There are a lot of different things to figure out, and we’re in this unbelievably strange and unstable moment in media.

But I do think we’ve figured out a model that is quality journalism built around great journalists, paired with really large scale convening that is building both great journalism and a really good business, a profitable business — which is something that is, to me as a former BuzzFeed executive, novel.

A profitable digital media business is in short supply these days. It’s funny, I was looking over our conversation from three years ago. You had just published your book Traffic, which was basically about what I would call the millennial digital media moment and everyone chasing massive scale.

“The platforms are going to deliver tons of traffic to us and then we’ll collect pennies and we’ll all get rich.” This was a pretty common thesis. It feels like you’re saying you’ve turned away from that. You’ve learned the lesson of that time.

Our chief revenue officer, Rachel Oppenheim, likes to joke that my next book will be called No Traffic, but we are really building an anti-scale business. The luxury of starting in that moment, in the rubble of the traffic apocalypse, was obviously not the path to success.

We had to think a lot about targeting and building a very specific audience. The thing that I have kind of come to realize in all these conversations… I listen to your show. We have a show about media that we yap about this on. What’s the future of media? Is it live? We were just talking about it. Who knows?

But in journalism, I have a lot of conviction that great stories aren’t going anywhere. The need for high-quality insight isn’t going anywhere. Great reporters aren’t going anywhere. What surface this all lives on is up for grabs, and you can’t be too ideological about that.

You say surface, I always say distribution.

Yeah.

A theme on Decoder that we come back to over and over again is your distribution shapes what you make. It’s just inevitable. The medium is the message, to borrow that framing. If surfaces — if distribution — are up for grabs, what are you holding onto?

I actually don’t buy that thesis, or at least I’m resisting that thesis because for the audience, the pull of distribution is incredibly powerful. The core thesis of BuzzFeed was we cracked the distribution and built for the distribution. Maybe I’m overreacting a little to that, but we definitely think all the time about how we want to reach political leaders and business leaders. We want to reach nonprofit leaders, and we want to reach people making decisions.

We want to reach them in person. We reach them a lot in email. We reach them on the web, we reach them in video, but we’re thinking about that same audience across media, and in fact, I think video is particularly interesting because of the pull. Videos are placed on the web in terms of the place you can get massive scale.

Then conversely, where there’s a pull of massive scale to create the biggest pull is just to be hyper-polarizing and find ways to create polarizing confrontation. That’s how you go viral, or one of the best ways at least, and we’re trying hard to build the discipline to resist that pull of distribution.

We’re already deep into the weeds. I hope that listeners can tell Ben and I like talking to each other about these things.

Please visit Semafor.com.

[Laughs] I’m excited to play some clips for you. So I’m glad that you said you were reacting to BuzzFeed. A few months ago we had Jonah Peretti on the show, and right after he had sold BuzzFeed to Byron Allen and the Weather Channel. There’s a lot going on there. In full disclosure to the audience, I literally had a beer with you just before I sat down with Jonah.

I remember.

I did not ask the questions you told me to ask, but he said—

Were they about running? That’s another show.

I didn’t do it. I was quickly in the weeds of Jonah as well, and I put to him what I think of as the original sin of digital media, which is that I think Jonah thought he could go so viral so consistently that he could crack distribution and that Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook would pay him money.

I’m going to play for you what he said to me in response to that, and I just want to get your reaction to it. Can we go ahead and play it?

Jonah Peretti: Yeah. I mean, first, just as a factual matter, we did get paid millions of dollars by Mark Zuckerberg. The prediction that they would pay for content was accurate, but it was just short-lived. So we got paid for that exploding watermelon.

Okay, so he said that to me and I said, “Yeah.”

That was a good day in the office.

It was a great day in the office, I’m guessing, but everyone knew that Mark Zuckerberg wasn’t going to pay forever.

I agree with Jonah on this. Looking back, we all say the social platforms were obviously going to always be dependent on UGC and never pay for anything, and these media companies building on social platforms never made any sense.

It’s worth remembering these investors’ experience had been shaped by cable, which was a different distribution platform in which companies like Viacom, ESPN, CNN, and MTV had built huge businesses on the back of this new distribution. So they said, “Here’s another new distribution. We’re going to build big businesses on the back of it.”

We now look back and say it was inevitable that Facebook would never pay for content, but it wasn’t. Facebook executives made choices at various times. They experimented with different things. If you are the person in charge of the success of the blue Facebook app, do you think, “It was a great decision to continually rely on low-quality YouTube generated content”? No, that thing is dying, obviously. They should have found a different path. It was a mistake.

Jonah made this argument to me as well, and this is the other—

Obviously I’m brainwashed by Jonah. I worked with him for a long time.

No, I’m just curious. Your paths have diverged and you are building a very different business. I’m just curious. This is the other clip from Jonah that I want to play for you. It is an argument that Facebook made a mistake. Here’s that clip:

Jonah Peretti: I actually believe that it was a mistake for Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg to not continue with the news tab, to not continue to pay professional content creators. These platforms have tons of resources and could have spent a couple of billion dollars a year on that, sustained a vibrant media ecosystem, really owned media in a way that would have been incredibly powerful for them and given them charisma, relevance, and authority that they just don’t have today.

The claim there is if Mark Zuckerberg had continued to fund BuzzFeed, he would have more charisma.

That the Facebook blue app would be more successful had they done different things? That’s pretty obvious. You could argue which things. That’s true, and then if you look at whether you would rather be Netflix or the blue Facebook app? You’d rather be Netflix, right?

Netflix famously doesn’t invest in these either.

Netflix pays a lot for content.

They pay a lot for content, but they don’t invest in news.

News, I agree. News is a complicated business. We’re a separate question. But they pay for a lot of professional content. YouTube is the biggest and most interesting story here because YouTube has found a way for individuals to build businesses on top of it in a really impressive way. There are occasional news creators like Johnny Harris, but he’s almost the exception that proves the rule, but we just had Kareem Rahma on our show.

These people are building real businesses, real careers, on top of YouTube, paying producers, increasingly moving up market.
